title: Weak lensing, big magnification: Recovering hidden lensing information from galaxy positions

paper.title: Weak lensing, big magnification: Recovering hidden lensing information from galaxy positions
paper.abstract: Abstract The combination of galaxy clustering and weak gravitational lensing is a powerful probe of cosmology, traditionally implemented through galaxy clustering and galaxy–galaxy lensing in a 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt analysis. An alternative lensing observable is the clustering cross-correlation of foreground and background galaxy samples induced by lensing magnification, but measurements of this signal have generally achieved lower signal-to-noise than shear-based lensing. We show that, for deep background samples selected from current photometric surveys, cancellation between galaxies with positive and negative magnification responses within the same sample can substantially reduce the achievable signal. Using DES Year 6 photometry and Balrog synthetic-source injections, we explore high-redshift ( z ≃ 0.7 z\simeq 0.7 – 2.5 2.5 ) galaxy samples split by the sign and amplitude of their magnification response. This separation reduces signal cancellation and can substantially increase both the magnification signal-to-noise and its cosmological constraining power. We refer to the resulting combination of foreground clustering and foreground–background cross-correlations with a response-selected background sample as BigMag. Forecasts based on DES-like simulated data vectors, adopting an optimistic sample configuration and sufficiently precise calibration of the magnification responses, show that BigMag can achieve constraining power comparable to traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt while relying only on galaxy positions. The same response-selected samples also enhance inverse galaxy–galaxy lensing (IGGL), a position–shear correlation dominated by magnification terms when the position sample lies behind the shape sample. Combining BigMag and IGGL self-calibrates the magnification responses further and yields marginalized S 8 S_{8} constraints comparable to traditional 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt analyses, and even tighter in the more precise magnification-calibration scenarios considered here. The framework also enables the construction of near-zero-magnification-response samples, with applications to traditional 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt and geometric lensing-ratio analyses. These results motivate further optimization and validation of galaxy selections to realize the potential of magnification as a complementary probe of cosmology.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Modern imaging surveys contain hundreds of millions of detected galaxies ( Bechtol et al., 2026 ) , and forthcoming experiments will increase this number to several billion ( Ivezić et al., 2019 ; Akeson et al., 2019 ; Euclid Collaboration et al., 2025c ; CSST Collaboration et al., 2026 ) . Yet only a fraction of these objects typically enter cosmological analyses ( DES Collaboration et al., 2026 , e.g.,) . The requirements imposed on a galaxy sample depend strongly on the observable for which it is used. Galaxy samples used for clustering (often referred to as lens or position samples) are generally restricted to relatively bright galaxies at low or intermediate redshift ( Weaverdyck et al., 2026 ) . Their observed number density can correlate with survey depth, seeing, sky brightness, stellar density, and other observing conditions. Because their autocorrelations are used to constrain galaxy bias and cosmology, these spatial variations must be accurately characterized and mitigated ( Rodríguez-Monroy et al., 2025 ) . Galaxy samples used for weak lensing shear (usually called source or shape samples) can extend to substantially fainter objects and higher redshifts, but require reliable galaxy shape measurements, shear calibration, and redshift characterization ( Yamamoto et al., 2025 ) . These requirements exclude many detected galaxies from either role. Weak lensing magnification offers a complementary way to exploit this broader galaxy population. By changing the observed solid angle and altering the apparent fluxes and sizes of background galaxies ( Bartelmann, 2010 ; Prat and Bacon, 2026 ) , magnification modulates their observed number density and the probability that they enter a selected sample. This signal can be isolated by cross-correlating foreground and background populations with minimal redshift overlap: physical clustering is then strongly suppressed, leaving a correlation dominated by the magnification of background galaxies by matter traced by the foreground sample. Like galaxy-galaxy lensing, this observable probes the foreground galaxy-matter connection, but uses background galaxy positions rather than shapes. Because the background population enters only through cross-correlations, its autocorrelation need not be modeled; provided the foreground density field is adequately corrected and residual imaging fluctuations are not correlated between the samples, background systematics increase the variance without biasing the mean signal. The background selection can therefore extend to deeper, denser samples, including galaxies without usable shapes, while the foreground sample remains subject to the usual clustering-systematics requirements. This work focuses on magnification-induced position–position correlations, which have been measured using a range of background populations ( Scranton et al., 2005 ; Hildebrandt et al., 2009 ; Morrison et al., 2012 ; Garcia-Fernandez et al., 2018 ; González-Nuevo et al., 2014 ) . Although well established, such measurements have generally achieved lower signal-to-noise than shape-based weak-lensing measurements ( Bernstein, 2009 ; Bartelmann, 2010 ; van Waerbeke, 2010 ; Joachimi and Bridle, 2010 ; Duncan et al., 2014 ; Mahony et al., 2022 ; Cueli et al., 2025 ) . One important and avoidable source of this reduced statistical power, recognised since the earliest quasar–galaxy analyses ( Ménard and Bartelmann, 2002 ) , is cancellation within conventionally selected background samples. A selected population responds through two competing effects: expansion of the observed area dilutes its surface density, while magnification of galaxy fluxes and sizes changes the number of objects satisfying the selection ( von Wietersheim-Kramsta et al., 2021 ; Elvin-Poole et al., 2023 ; Legnani et al., 2026 ) . The net response can therefore be positive, negative, or close to zero, and a conventional sample may combine populations with opposite responses whose lensing signals partially cancel. Separating these populations preserves the oppositely signed contributions and also helps distinguish magnification from residual intrinsic clustering: the magnification signal reverses sign between the samples, whereas clustering caused by redshift overlap does not ( Hildebrandt et al., 2009 , e.g.) . Crucially, the magnification response is a property that can be estimated before measuring the cosmological cross-correlation. Catalogue-level perturbations have been used to propagate artificial magnification through the complex selection of spectroscopic samples and through flux-dependent photometric-redshift assignment ( Wenzl et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2025a ) . Image-level synthetic-source injection methods, such as Balrog , extend this logic through detection and measurement: simulated galaxies are magnified by a known amount, injected into real survey images, and processed through the same detection, measurement, and selection pipeline as the data ( Suchyta et al., 2016 ; Everett et al., 2022 ; Anbajagane et al., 2025 ) . The change in the number of selected objects then provides a direct calibration of the sample-selection response ( Elvin-Poole et al., 2023 ; Legnani et al., 2026 ) . A self-organizing map (SOM) ( Myles et al., 2021 ; Giannini et al., 2025 ; Yin et al., 2025 ) offers a natural representation of this information: cells containing galaxies with similar observed colors and magnitudes can be assigned both a redshift distribution and a magnification response. The SOM can then be used to construct high-redshift samples whose responses have a controlled sign and amplitude while maintaining the required redshift separation from the foreground sample. In this work, we use injection-calibrated responses not only to calibrate a given selection but to define it. We split high-redshift galaxy samples into populations with positive and negative net magnification responses in the multi-dimensional colour–magnitude space of the SOM. Treating these populations as separate density fields prevents their signals from cancelling and provides cross-correlations with opposite signs around the same foreground structures. We call the combination of foreground clustering and its cross-correlation with these dense, response-optimized background samples BigMag. Its structure closely parallels that of a traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt analysis ( Porredon et al., 2022 ; Pandey et al., 2022 ) . In both cases, the foreground autocorrelation constrains the combination of galaxy bias and matter clustering, while a lensing cross-correlation breaks the degeneracy between galaxy bias and the cosmological fluctuation amplitude. Traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt uses galaxy–galaxy lensing for this purpose; BigMag instead uses magnification-induced correlations between galaxy positions. The amplitude calibration provided by the magnification coefficient consequently plays a role analogous (although not identical) to the multiplicative shear calibration in galaxy–galaxy lensing. The same response-selected high-redshift samples also enhance inverse galaxy–galaxy lensing (IGGL) ( Cross and Sánchez, 2024 ) . In the IGGL configuration, the galaxy-position sample lies behind the source-shape sample. The conventional density–shear contribution is then strongly suppressed, and the position–shear correlation is dominated by the correlation between the magnification of the high-redshift position sample and the shear of the foreground source sample, together with the corresponding intrinsic-alignment contribution. BigMag and IGGL depend on the same magnification coefficients but probe them through different correlations and redshift kernels. Their combination can therefore partially self-calibrate the magnification responses while simultaneously constraining cosmology. It also provides a valuable consistency test because the two observables have different dependencies on galaxy bias, shear calibration, intrinsic alignments, and observational systematics. We demonstrate this approach using DES Year 6 photometry, Balrog synthetic-source injections, and SOM-based redshift calibration to construct galaxy selections with controlled redshift distributions and magnification responses. We then use DES-informed number densities, redshift distributions, and response coefficients to generate simulated clustering and weak-lensing data vectors. These forecasts quantify the gain from separating positive- and negative-response populations, compare BigMag with traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt, and study the additional information supplied by IGGL. We also compare the combined magnification observables with cosmic shear and standard 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt analyses. Finally, we investigate the calibration precision required for the magnification coefficients, the sensitivity of the measurement to residual redshift overlap, and the information available from magnification ratios on scales excluded from the fiducial cosmological analysis. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the magnification contribution to galaxy-density correlations, motivates response-based sample selection, and discusses IGGL and sensitivity to observational systematics. Section 3 presents the DES Year 6 and Balrog data products, explores magnitude- and SOM-based selections, and describes the simulated data vectors. Section 4 presents the cosmological forecasts for BigMag and IGGL and their comparison and combination with traditional weak-lensing probes. We then discuss the implications and requirements for applying the method to data and summarize our conclusions. The appendices provide further tests of magnification-response selection and calibration, assess the impact of redshift overlap, explore small-scale magnification ratios, and derive the treatment of a redshift-dependent magnification response.

sections.heading: 2 Theory and motivation
sections.text: This section develops the theoretical framework for the magnification observables used in this work. We describe how intrinsic clustering and weak-lensing magnification contribute to galaxy density correlations, motivating background-galaxy selections based on their magnification response. We then discuss magnification in galaxy–galaxy lensing, focusing on the inverse configuration, and assess the impact of observational systematics.

The first term, C area = − 2 C_{\mathrm{area}}=-2 , arises from the stretching of the sky area and always acts to dilute the observed number density. To this end, we need to consider the observed galaxy density in the sky, δ g obs \delta_{g}^{\text{obs}} , defined for different galaxy selections (e.g., distinct redshift bins or samples at similar redshifts but selected by other properties). Second, the convergence field at the redshift of the foreground sample does not correlate with the intrinsic density of the background sample, ⟨ κ i ​ δ m , j ⟩ ≃ 0 \langle\kappa_{i}\,\delta_{m,j}\rangle\simeq 0 . Finally, the convergence–convergence term is typically subdominant on the angular scales of interest. Under these assumptions, the observed cross-correlation reduces to ⟨ δ g , i obs ​ δ g , j obs ⟩ ≃ b i ​ C mag , ​ j ​ ⟨ κ j ​ δ m , i ⟩ . \left\langle\delta_{g,i}^{\mathrm{obs}}\,\delta_{g,j}^{\mathrm{obs}}\right\rangle\simeq b_{i}C_{\mathrm{mag,\emph{j}}}\left\langle\kappa_{j}\,\delta_{m,i}\right\rangle. (13) This remaining term describes the correlation between the matter density field traced by foreground galaxies and the convergence field sourced by the same large-scale structure along the line of sight to the background sample. In this sense, Eq. ( 13 ) highlights the three key ingredients required to extract cosmological information from magnification-induced galaxy cross-correlations: 1. The galaxy bias of the foreground sample, b i b_{i} ; 2. The magnification response of the background sample, also called magnification coefficient, C mag , ​ j C_{\mathrm{mag,\emph{j}}} ; 3. The matter–convergence correlation, ⟨ κ j ​ δ m , i ⟩ \langle\kappa_{j}\,\delta_{m,i}\rangle , which contains the cosmological information given the redshift distribution of each galaxy sample. Two important notes are in order here. On the one hand, the galaxy bias parameter, b i b_{i} , is a property of the foreground (low-redshift) sample, it will generally be positive ( b i ≥ 1 b_{i}\geq 1 for typical galaxy samples) and cannot be known a priori but should be constrained using the galaxy auto-correlation of that foreground sample. On the other hand, the magnification parameter C mag , ​ j C_{\mathrm{mag,\emph{j}}} is a property of the background (high-redshift) sample and can be estimated independently using sample-selection response techniques, in particular synthetic source injection (SSI) algorithms, such as Balrog in DES ( Suchyta et al., 2016 ; Everett et al., 2022 ) . Crucially, the magnification coefficient can be positive, negative, or zero depending on the value of C sample , ​ j C_{\mathrm{sample,\emph{j}}} , according to Eq. ( 10 ). Therefore, given that galaxy bias is positive, the sign of C mag , ​ j C_{\mathrm{mag,\emph{j}}} (which can be characterized a priori ) will determine the sign of magnification-induced galaxy cross-correlations. To leading order in the convergence, the observed autocorrelation of foreground bin i i can be written as ⟨ δ g , i obs ​ δ g , i obs ⟩ = b i 2 ​ ⟨ δ m , i ​ δ m , i ⟩ + 2 ​ b i ​ C mag , i ​ ⟨ δ m , i ​ κ i ⟩ + 𝒪 ⁡ ( κ 2 ) . \left\langle\delta_{g,i}^{\mathrm{obs}}\delta_{g,i}^{\mathrm{obs}}\right\rangle=b_{i}^{2}\left\langle\delta_{m,i}\delta_{m,i}\right\rangle+2b_{i}C_{\mathrm{mag},i}\left\langle\delta_{m,i}\kappa_{i}\right\rangle+\mathcal{O}(\kappa^{2}). (14) For typical low-redshift lens samples and on the angular scales considered in this work, the magnification contribution to the auto-correlation is subdominant with respect to the intrinsic clustering term. The auto-correlation can therefore be approximated as ⟨ δ g , i obs ​ δ g , i obs ⟩ ≃ b i 2 ​ ⟨ δ m , i ​ δ m , i ⟩ , \left\langle\delta_{g,i}^{\mathrm{obs}}\,\delta_{g,i}^{\mathrm{obs}}\right\rangle\simeq b_{i}^{2}\left\langle\delta_{m,i}\,\delta_{m,i}\right\rangle, (15) allowing the galaxy bias of the foreground sample to be constrained directly from its clustering signal. Taken together, Eqs. ( 13 ) and ( 15 ) show that cosmological information can be obtained 2 2 2 These simplifications are introduced for qualitative and pedagogical clarity; the theoretical predictions used in subsequent sections include the full set of intrinsic-clustering and magnification contributions. from the joint analysis of the auto-correlation of a foreground galaxy sample and its cross-correlation with a background sample in a non-overlapping redshift bin. In this configuration, the auto-correlation primarily constrains the galaxy bias of the foreground sample, while the cross-correlation isolates the magnification-induced signal that probes the matter distribution along the line of sight and depends linearly on the magnification coefficient of the background galaxies. Two key implications follow from this framework, which form the main motivation for the analysis presented in this paper: • The magnification coefficient of background galaxies, which sets the amplitude (and sign) of the cross-correlation signal, can be estimated a priori for galaxy samples using synthetic source injection (SSI) techniques, such as Balrog . This enables the design and optimisation of sample selections that maximise the magnification signal, an aspect that is particularly important in the presence of mixed populations that would otherwise lead to partial cancellation between negative and positive magnification contributions. We explore this strategy in detail in § 2.3 . • Because the analysis does not require the auto-correlation of the background sample, the cosmological inference is significantly less sensitive to observational systematics affecting that sample. This relaxes the requirements on systematics mitigation for the background galaxies, allowing for more aggressive selections and the inclusion of a larger number of objects. The impact of observational systematics in this context is discussed in § 2.5 .

Galaxies with C sample < 2 C_{\mathrm{sample}}<2 produce a negative magnification-induced cross-correlation ( × \times -corr.), those with C sample = 2 C_{\mathrm{sample}}=2 yield a null signal, and galaxies with C sample > 2 C_{\mathrm{sample}}>2 produce a positive magnification-induced cross-correlation. The foreground and background samples have mean redshifts ⟨ z ⟩ = 0.34 \langle z\rangle=0.34 and 1.70 1.70 , respectively, with DES Y6-informed number densities. The foreground magnification response is set to zero throughout. Left: the unsplit background configuration without magnification ( C mag = 0 C_{\rm mag}=0 , open circles) and with its adopted response ( C mag = − 0.29 C_{\rm mag}=-0.29 , grey squares). The latter yields S / N = 10.2 S/N=10.2 over the displayed angular range; the inset highlights the small-scale signal. Right: configurations with positive and negative background responses, C mag = + 1.60 C_{\rm mag}=+1.60 (rose circles) and − 1.90 -1.90 (blue squares), yield S / N = 44.1 S/N=44.1 and 54.0 54.0 , respectively. Points show model predictions, with error bars from the diagonal of the simulated covariance; the quoted signal-to-noise values include correlations between angular bins. These illustrative configurations show the potential gain from separately measuring populations with opposite magnification responses. Building on the framework above, we now consider how background-galaxy selections can be designed to enhance sensitivity to magnification. Because the magnification-induced cross-correlation scales linearly with C mag C_{\mathrm{mag}} , Eq. ( 13 ), broad selections can combine galaxies with positive, negative, and near-zero responses whose contributions partially cancel, reducing the signal-to-noise ratio (Figure 2 ). This motivates grouping background galaxies according to the sign and magnitude of C mag C_{\mathrm{mag}} , so that their contributions add coherently. Since C mag C_{\mathrm{mag}} can be characterized using sample-selection response techniques such as synthetic source injections, these response-based selections can be constructed and optimized in practice. The principle is the same as in ( α − 1 ) (\alpha-1) -weighted estimators ( Ménard and Bartelmann, 2002 ; Scranton et al., 2005 ) , here applied to responses calibrated for arbitrary selections rather than inferred from the number-count slope, and with the resulting groups kept as separate fields rather than combined into a single weighted sample. Figure 3 illustrates this gain using a simulated clustering cross-correlation between foreground and background samples at z = 0.34 z=0.34 and z = 1.7 z=1.7 , like those from Fig. 1 , with number densities informed by DES Y6 (more details about this in § 3 ). In the absence of magnification, the cross-correlation of the foreground and background samples is null, as expected, since they do not overlap in redshift. When considering magnification, an unsplit background sample, like the one depicted in Fig. 2 , produces a magnification signal with modest signal-to-noise because of partial cancellation (left panel). Splitting the same background parent population into subsamples with positive and negative magnification responses substantially increases the signal-to-noise of the measurement (right panel). The construction of these samples from real data is described in § 3 . Opposite-response subsamples also provide an internal consistency test of the origin of the signal. The leading magnification-induced correlation changes sign with C mag C_{\rm mag} , whereas obscuration and dust extinction dim background galaxies ( Ménard et al., 2010 ) and can reduce the observed background counts without following this sign reversal ( Hildebrandt et al., 2013 ; Gaztanaga et al., 2021 ) . Comparing subsamples around the same foreground galaxies, while accounting for differences in their redshift distributions and selection, can therefore help distinguish magnification from observational contamination. On the other hand, samples with C mag ≃ 0 C_{\rm mag}\simeq 0 provide a complementary null test of the leading magnification contribution, and they would also have applications beyond these consistency tests. The same response-calibration and selection machinery used here to enhance magnification can instead be used to construct samples with a total magnification response close to zero in each tomographic bin. Applied to the galaxy-position samples in 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt analyses, this would suppress lens-magnification contributions to galaxy clustering and galaxy–galaxy lensing, reducing their sensitivity to magnification modelling and response-calibration uncertainties ( Euclid Collaboration et al., 2022 ; Elvin-Poole et al., 2023 ; Legnani et al., 2026 ) . Furthermore, null-response lens samples would be particularly valuable for lensing ratio measurements ( Jain and Taylor, 2003 ; Prat et al., 2019 ; Unruh et al., 2019 ) , where the contributions from magnification can reduce the geometrical nature that makes these measurements so interesting. Having established the motivation for response-based selections, we next discuss their relevance to inverse galaxy–galaxy lensing and the impact of observational systematics on these observables.

sections.heading: 2.4 (Inverse) Galaxy-galaxy lensing
sections.text: Another measurement that can be dominated by weak lensing magnification in particular redshift configurations is galaxy-galaxy lensing (GGL, Kaiser 1992 ). The GGL observable is the cross-correlation between the observed galaxy density of a position sample, δ g obs \delta_{g}^{\mathrm{obs}} , defined in Eq. ( 11 ), and the observed ellipticity of a shape sample, e obs e^{\mathrm{obs}} . In the weak-lensing regime, the latter can be modeled as the sum of the gravitational shear and the intrinsic galaxy ellipticity ( Sánchez et al., 2022 ) , e obs = γ + e int , \displaystyle e^{\text{obs}}=\gamma+e^{\text{int}}, (16) where | γ | ≪ 1 |\gamma|\ll 1 . Correlating δ g obs \delta_{g}^{\text{obs}} with e obs e^{\text{obs}} to get the relevant cross-correlation for GGL, we get four terms representing different physical effects: ⟨ δ g obs ​ e obs ⟩ = ⟨ ( δ g int + C mag ​ κ ) ​ ( γ + e int ) ⟩ = = ⟨ δ g int ​ γ ⟩ ⏟ trad GGL + C mag ​ ⟨ κ ​ γ ⟩ ⏟ lens mag + ⟨ δ g int ​ e int ⟩ ⏟ IA + C mag ​ ⟨ κ ​ e int ⟩ . ⏟ lens mag + IA \begin{split}&\left<\delta_{g}^{\text{obs}}e^{\text{obs}}\right>=\left<(\delta_{g}^{\text{int}}+C_{\mathrm{mag}}\kappa)\,(\gamma+e^{\rm int})\right>=\\ &=\underbrace{\left<\delta_{g}^{\text{int}}\gamma\right>}_{\text{trad GGL}}+\,\underbrace{C_{\mathrm{mag}}\left<\kappa\,\gamma\right>}_{\text{lens mag}}+\,\underbrace{\left<\delta_{g}^{\text{int}}e^{\rm int}\right>}_{\text{IA}}+\,\underbrace{C_{\mathrm{mag}}\left<\kappa\,e^{\rm int}\right>.}_{\text{lens mag + IA}}\end{split} (17) In the traditional GGL configuration, the position (lens) sample lies at lower redshift than the shape (source) sample, and the first term in Eq. ( 17 ) dominates. To make magnification the leading contribution, this ordering can be reversed by placing the position sample behind the shape sample. In that case, the first term in Eq. ( 17 ) vanishes, and the measurement only depends on weak lensing and intrinsic alignments (IA). This configuration is known as Inverse Galaxy-Galaxy Lensing (IGGL) and is studied in detail by Cross and Sánchez (2024) . Later in this work, we combine IGGL with the clustering cross-correlations described in § 2.2 to constrain cosmology using weak-lensing magnification.

sections.heading: 2.5 Impact of observational systematics
sections.text: Having seen how galaxy samples can be selected and optimized according to their magnification coefficients, we now consider the impact of observational systematics on these measurements and selections. In practice, the observed galaxy density field is affected by observational systematics arising from spatial variations of survey depth, seeing, sky brightness, stellar contamination, and other imaging-related effects. These systematics can be modeled schematically as additive and multiplicative contributions to the observed galaxy density contrast ( Weaverdyck and Huterer, 2021 ; Berlfein et al., 2024 ) , δ g obs = ( 1 + m g ) ​ δ g true + s g , \delta_{g}^{\mathrm{obs}}=(1+m_{g})\,\delta_{g}^{\mathrm{true}}+s_{g}, (18) where δ g true \delta_{g}^{\mathrm{true}} denotes the systematics-free physical density contrast, including intrinsic clustering and lensing magnification (see Eq. 11 ), while m g m_{g} and s g s_{g} represent multiplicative and additive systematic fields, respectively. For the qualitative discussion below, we assume that m g m_{g} and s g s_{g} have zero mean and are statistically uncorrelated with the cosmological density field. This assumption is appropriate for instrumental or Galactic contaminants in an ensemble sense, but excludes effects tied directly to foreground structure, such as blending and obscuration, which must be included explicitly in a complete analysis (see the discussion in § 5.4 ). When considering the clustering auto-correlation of a given galaxy sample, observational systematics enter at leading order. Using Eq. ( 18 ), the observed auto-correlation can be written schematically as ⟨ δ g obs ​ δ g obs ⟩ \displaystyle\langle\delta_{g}^{\rm obs}\delta_{g}^{\rm obs}\rangle = ( 1 + ⟨ m g ​ m g ⟩ ) ​ ⟨ δ g true ​ δ g true ⟩ \displaystyle=\left(1+\langle m_{g}m_{g}\rangle\right)\langle\delta_{g}^{\rm true}\delta_{g}^{\rm true}\rangle + ⟨ s g ​ s g ⟩ + 𝒪 ⁡ ( m g ​ s g ) . \displaystyle\quad+\langle s_{g}s_{g}\rangle+\mathcal{O}(m_{g}s_{g}). (19) As a result, multiplicative systematics rescale the intrinsic clustering amplitude, while additive systematics contribute their own spatial correlations. Accurate cosmological inference from the foreground-sample auto-correlation therefore requires these observational systematics to be carefully characterized and mitigated ( Weaverdyck and Huterer, 2021 ; Berlfein et al., 2024 ; Rodríguez-Monroy et al., 2025 ) We now consider the cross-correlation between a foreground sample i i and a background sample j j in non-overlapping redshift bins, as discussed in § 2.2 . Provided that the foreground sample is adequately corrected for observational systematics ( δ g , i obs ≈ δ g , i true \delta_{g,i}^{\mathrm{obs}}\approx\delta_{g,i}^{\mathrm{true}} ), any residual additive or multiplicative contamination in the background sample does not correlate with the intrinsic density of the foreground galaxies. In this case, the expectation value of the observed cross-correlation remains unbiased, ⟨ δ g , i obs ​ δ g , j obs ⟩ \displaystyle\langle\delta_{g,i}^{\rm obs}\delta_{g,j}^{\rm obs}\rangle = ⟨ δ g , i true ​ ( 1 + m g , j ) ​ δ g , j true ⟩ + ⟨ δ g , i true ​ s g , j ⟩ \displaystyle=\left\langle\delta_{g,i}^{\rm true}(1+m_{g,j})\delta_{g,j}^{\rm true}\right\rangle+\left\langle\delta_{g,i}^{\rm true}s_{g,j}\right\rangle ≃ ⟨ δ g , i true ​ δ g , j true ⟩ . \displaystyle\simeq\left\langle\delta_{g,i}^{\mathrm{true}}\,\delta_{g,j}^{\mathrm{true}}\right\rangle. (20) Therefore, the magnification-induced cross-correlation does not require the background sample to be free of observational systematics in order to obtain an unbiased cross-correlation signal. However, although the mean cross-correlation is unaffected, residual systematics in the background sample can increase the variance of the measurement. To illustrate this, we consider the case where the foreground sample is well corrected, δ g , i obs ≃ δ g , i true \delta_{g,i}^{\mathrm{obs}}\simeq\delta_{g,i}^{\mathrm{true}} , while the background sample contains residual additive and multiplicative contaminants, as in Eq. ( 18 ). For the calculation, we define X ≡ δ g , i obs ​ δ g , j obs ≃ δ g , i true ​ [ ( 1 + m g , j ) ​ δ g , j true + s g , j ] . X\equiv\delta_{g,i}^{\mathrm{obs}}\,\delta_{g,j}^{\mathrm{obs}}\simeq\delta_{g,i}^{\mathrm{true}}\Big[(1+m_{g,j})\,\delta_{g,j}^{\mathrm{true}}+s_{g,j}\Big]. (21) Under the assumptions stated above (in particular that m g , j m_{g,j} and s g , j s_{g,j} do not correlate with the cosmological density field), ⟨ X ⟩ ≃ ⟨ δ g , i true ​ δ g , j true ⟩ \langle X\rangle\simeq\langle\delta_{g,i}^{\mathrm{true}}\delta_{g,j}^{\mathrm{true}}\rangle , i.e. the mean cross-correlation remains unbiased. The variance, Var ⁡ ( X ) = ⟨ X 2 ⟩ − ⟨ X ⟩ 2 \mathrm{Var}(X)=\langle X^{2}\rangle-\langle X\rangle^{2} , however, receives additional contributions. Neglecting cross-terms between additive and multiplicative contaminants for simplicity, and assuming that m g , j m_{g,j} is statistically independent of the cosmological fields, we obtain ⟨ X 2 ⟩ \displaystyle\langle X^{2}\rangle ≃ ⟨ ( 1 + m g , j ) 2 ⟩ ​ ⟨ ( δ g , i true ​ δ g , j true ) 2 ⟩ \displaystyle\simeq\langle(1+m_{g,j})^{2}\rangle\left\langle(\delta_{g,i}^{\rm true}\delta_{g,j}^{\rm true})^{2}\right\rangle + ⟨ ( δ g , i true ​ s g , j ) 2 ⟩ . \displaystyle\quad+\left\langle(\delta_{g,i}^{\rm true}s_{g,j})^{2}\right\rangle. (22) and therefore Var ⁡ ( X ) \displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(X) ≃ ⟨ ( 1 + m g , j ) 2 ⟩ ​ Var ​ ( δ g , i true ​ δ g , j true ) \displaystyle\simeq\langle(1+m_{g,j})^{2}\rangle\,\mathrm{Var}\!\left(\delta_{g,i}^{\rm true}\delta_{g,j}^{\rm true}\right) + Var ⁡ ( δ g , i true ​ s g , j ) \displaystyle\quad+\mathrm{Var}\!\left(\delta_{g,i}^{\rm true}s_{g,j}\right) + Var ⁡ ( m g , j ) ​ ⟨ δ g , i true ​ δ g , j true ⟩ 2 + ⋯ . \displaystyle\quad+\mathrm{Var}(m_{g,j})\left\langle\delta_{g,i}^{\rm true}\delta_{g,j}^{\rm true}\right\rangle^{2}+\cdots. (23) For a mean-subtracted multiplicative field, ⟨ m g , j ⟩ = 0 \langle m_{g,j}\rangle=0 , the prefactor reduces to ⟨ ( 1 + m g , j ) 2 ⟩ = 1 + ⟨ m g , j 2 ⟩ \langle(1+m_{g,j})^{2}\rangle=1+\langle m_{g,j}^{2}\rangle , making explicit that multiplicative residuals rescale the variance of the true cross-correlation measurement. Similarly, the remaining terms contribute to the increase in the measurement variance (and thus the covariance of the estimated cross-correlation), degrading the statistical precision. Since the background sample enters the analysis only through cross-correlations, and its auto-correlation is not required for cosmological inference, this framework allows for more aggressive binning strategies at high redshift. In particular, the background sample can be extended to the full depth of the survey without stringent systematics mitigation requirements. At the same time, accurate correction of observational systematics in the foreground sample remains essential, as its auto-correlation is used to constrain the galaxy bias. The impact of observational systematics on the IGGL observable can be understood similarly. In this configuration the galaxy position sample acts as the background field of the cross-correlation and may contain residual multiplicative and additive contaminants, δ g obs = ( 1 + m g ) ​ δ g true + s g , \delta_{g}^{\mathrm{obs}}=(1+m_{g})\,\delta_{g}^{\mathrm{true}}+s_{g}, (24) while the shape sample is assumed to be well calibrated. Expanding the estimator, ⟨ δ g obs ​ e obs ⟩ = ⟨ [ ( 1 + m g ) ​ δ g true + s g ] ​ ( γ + e int ) ⟩ , \langle\delta_{g}^{\mathrm{obs}}e^{\mathrm{obs}}\rangle=\left\langle\big[(1+m_{g})\delta_{g}^{\mathrm{true}}+s_{g}\big](\gamma+e^{\mathrm{int}})\right\rangle, (25) and assuming that m g m_{g} and s g s_{g} do not correlate with the cosmological density or shear fields, all mixed terms vanish. The expectation value therefore reduces to the standard IGGL contribution, and the mean signal remains unbiased. However, residual multiplicative and additive contaminants increase the variance of the estimator through terms proportional to ⟨ m g 2 ⟩ \langle m_{g}^{2}\rangle and ⟨ s g ​ s g ⟩ \langle s_{g}s_{g}\rangle , inflating the covariance without biasing the mean measurement.

sections.heading: 3 Data and simulations
sections.text: This section describes the data products and galaxy selections used to motivate the BigMag forecasts. The empirical and forecast components play distinct roles. First, DES Year 6 photometry, DES Year 6 Balrog synthetic-source injections, and SOMPZ redshift calibration are used to identify well-separated foreground and background populations and to measure how the number-density response to magnification varies within the high-redshift population. A simple magnitude partition provides direct evidence that positive and negative magnification contributions can partially cancel in an unsplit sample. Second, we explore a self-organizing map (SOM) as a more general representation in which both the redshift distribution and magnification response can be associated with regions of colour–magnitude space. The present Balrog campaign, however, does not provide sufficient statistics for an unbiased optimization of the response of every individual SOM cell. We therefore distinguish the response separation demonstrated by externally defined magnitude cuts from the larger, noisier apparent separation obtained by ranking SOM cells. Finally, we construct simulated data vectors with DES-informed redshifts and number densities, but with optimistic target magnification responses. The cosmological forecasts should consequently be interpreted as conditional forecasts of the information available if future, larger injection campaigns can construct and calibrate samples with this level of response separation.

sections.heading: 3.1 DES Y6 samples and Balrog injections
sections.text: We start from the public DES Y6 Gold photometric catalog ( Bechtol et al., 2026 ) and the corresponding DES Y6 Balrog synthetic-source injection catalogs ( Anbajagane et al., 2025 ) . To generate realistic injected sources, Balrog uses galaxy models fitted to observations from the DES Y3 deep fields ( Hartley et al., 2022 ) . These synthetic galaxies are injected into the real DES images, after which the same detection, deblending, and measurement pipeline used for the survey data is rerun. This procedure provides an empirical characterization of the survey transfer function: for a galaxy with known injected properties, we can determine whether it is detected, how its properties are measured in the wide-field data, and which sample selection it enters. This information is a key ingredient in both the SOMPZ redshift calibration and the magnification-response calibration, which are formulated in terms of observed galaxy properties. For the magnification calibration we use two Balrog runs from Anbajagane et al. (2025) . The fiducial run contains the unmodified injected galaxies. The magnified run contains the same underlying injected galaxies after applying a small positive magnification with convergence Δ ​ κ = 0.01 \Delta\kappa=0.01 to their fluxes and sizes. We apply the same catalog-level cuts to both measured catalogs: FLAGS_GOLD=0 , FLAGS_FOOTPRINT=1 , FLAGS_FOREGROUND=0 , and EXT_MASH>=2 . We use the dereddened measured i i -band magnitude for magnitude selections, and assign each detected object to a 32 × 32 32\times 32 wide-field SOM cell trained on DES wide-field g ​ r ​ i ​ z griz photometry. The sample-selection response is estimated from weighted number counts. If S S denotes a selected set of wide SOM cells and a possible magnitude range, the fiducial and magnified counts are N ^ r ​ ( S ) = ∑ j ∈ D r ​ ( S ) 1 N inj , j , r ∈ { fid , mag } , \widehat{N}_{r}(S)=\sum_{j\in D_{r}(S)}\frac{1}{N_{{\rm inj},j}},\qquad r\in\{\mathrm{fid},\mathrm{mag}\}, (26) where D r ​ ( S ) D_{r}(S) is the set of detected Balrog objects in run r r that pass the selection, and N inj , j N_{{\rm inj},j} is the number of attempted injections of the corresponding underlying deep-field object. The factor 1 / N inj 1/N_{\rm inj} ensures that objects injected more often do not receive disproportionate weight. We then define ( Elvin-Poole et al., 2023 ; Legnani et al., 2026 ) : C ^ sample ​ ( S ) = N ^ mag ​ ( S ) − N ^ fid ​ ( S ) N ^ fid ​ ( S ) ​ Δ ​ κ . \widehat{C}_{\rm sample}(S)=\frac{\widehat{N}_{\rm mag}(S)-\widehat{N}_{\rm fid}(S)}{\widehat{N}_{\rm fid}(S)\,\Delta\kappa}. (27) The geometric area term contributes − 2 ​ κ -2\kappa to the observed number-density contrast, so that C mag = C sample − 2 C_{\rm mag}=C_{\rm sample}-2 is the net magnification response. Thus C sample = 2 C_{\rm sample}=2 is the null-response boundary, and positive and negative C mag C_{\rm mag} produce oppositely signed magnification contributions. For estimates of C sample C_{\rm sample} and its covariance, we restrict the fiducial Balrog detections to the same set of wide-field tiles as the magnified run. This matched-footprint choice removes changes in the count ratio caused by different survey areas rather than by magnifying the same parent population. In contrast, the redshift calibration uses the full fiducial Balrog footprint, because it is intended to estimate the redshift distribution of the survey sample rather than the response of the matched magnification sub-footprint. We estimate statistical uncertainties on C sample C_{\rm sample} with a spatial delete-one jackknife. We construct K K TreeCorr patches ( Jarvis et al., 2004 ) from the positions of the magnified injections and assign both fiducial and magnified detections to these fixed patches. Let N ^ r , k ​ ( S ) \widehat{N}_{r,k}(S) be the weighted count in patch k k . The leave-one-out counts and response are N ^ r , − k ​ ( S ) \displaystyle\widehat{N}_{r,-k}(S) = N ^ r ​ ( S ) − N ^ r , k ​ ( S ) , \displaystyle=\widehat{N}_{r}(S)-\widehat{N}_{r,k}(S), (28) C ^ sample , − k ​ ( S ) \displaystyle\widehat{C}_{{\rm sample},-k}(S) = N ^ mag , − k ​ ( S ) − N ^ fid , − k ​ ( S ) N ^ fid , − k ​ ( S ) ​ Δ ​ κ . \displaystyle=\frac{\widehat{N}_{{\rm mag},-k}(S)-\widehat{N}_{{\rm fid},-k}(S)}{\widehat{N}_{{\rm fid},-k}(S)\,\Delta\kappa}. (29) The corresponding jackknife variance is then σ JK 2 ​ ( C sample ) \displaystyle\sigma^{2}_{\rm JK}\!\left(C_{\rm sample}\right) = K − 1 K ​ ∑ k = 1 K [ C ^ sample , − k − C ¯ sample JK ] 2 , \displaystyle=\frac{K-1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left[\widehat{C}_{{\rm sample},-k}-\overline{C}_{\rm sample}^{\rm JK}\right]^{2}, (30) C ¯ sample JK \displaystyle\qquad\overline{C}_{\rm sample}^{\rm JK} = 1 K ​ ∑ k = 1 K C ^ sample , − k . \displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\widehat{C}_{{\rm sample},-k}. (31) This construction preserves the nonlinear ratio in Eq. ( 27 ) for every leave-one-out realization. These jackknife uncertainties characterize the response of a fixed selection. They do not by themselves include the additional uncertainty or selection bias that arises when the same noisy cell responses are used to define that selection. Figure 4: Self-organizing map (SOM) of DES Year 6 galaxies used to construct the redshift- and magnification-selected samples. Each pixel corresponds to a SOM cell defined from the observed galaxy fluxes. The top panel shows the mean redshift, ⟨ z ⟩ \langle z\rangle , of the galaxies assigned to each cell, revealing the redshift structure across the color–magnitude manifold. The bottom panel shows the corresponding sample-selection magnification response, C sample C_{\rm sample} , estimated with Balrog synthetic injections. The color scale for C sample C_{\rm sample} is centered on C sample = 2 C_{\rm sample}=2 , the value at which the sample-selection response cancels the geometric area term in the observed number density. Cells with different values of C sample C_{\rm sample} can be combined to build samples with positive, negative, or near-null magnification response at fixed redshift. These SOM maps therefore provide the basis for the high-redshift H + and H - selections used in the simulated data vectors.

sections.heading: 3.2 A SOM representation of redshift and magnification response
sections.text: We use a SOM representation to compress the galaxy color-magnitude space into cells for which redshift and magnification response can be calibrated. The wide SOM is trained on DES wide-field g ​ r ​ i ​ z griz photometry and contains 32 × 32 32\times 32 cells, denoted c ^ \hat{c} . This produces a two-dimensional map of the galaxy population in which each cell carries the quantities needed for the magnification analysis: c ^ ⟶ { n c ^ ​ ( z ) , z ¯ c ^ , n gal c ^ , C mag c ^ } . \hat{c}\quad\longrightarrow\quad\left\{n_{\hat{c}}(z),\;\bar{z}_{\hat{c}},\;n_{\rm gal}^{\hat{c}},\;C_{\rm mag}^{\hat{c}}\right\}. (32) Here z ¯ c ^ \bar{z}_{\hat{c}} is the estimated mean redshift for the cell and n gal c ^ n_{\rm gal}^{\hat{c}} is the angular number density. The magnification coefficient C mag c ^ C_{\rm mag}^{\hat{c}} is estimated from Balrog counts as explained in § 3.1 . For the redshift calibration we also use a deep SOM, denoted c c , trained on the DES deep-field optical and near-infrared photometry. The deep-field catalog is restricted to objects passing the deep field mask and flag cuts, and we keep objects classified as galaxies by the deep-field nearest-neighbor classifier. Deep objects are matched to redshift information from the DES redshift calibration sample when available, while the Balrog transfer function links their deep-field properties to their measured wide-field SOM cells. The SOMPZ calibration follows the DES Y3 and DES Y6 methodology ( Buchs et al., 2019 ; Myles et al., 2021 ; Sánchez et al., 2023 ; Campos et al., 2024 ; Giannini et al., 2024 ; Giannini et al., 2025 ; Yin et al., 2025 ) . For a sample defined in wide cells, the redshift distribution of a target ensemble is written as a mixture over deep SOM cells, p ⁡ ( z ∣ S ) = ∑ c ^ ∈ S p ⁡ ( c ^ ∣ S ) ​ ∑ c p ⁡ ( z ∣ c , c ^ , S ) ​ p ​ ( c ∣ c ^ , S ) , p(z\mid S)=\sum_{\hat{c}\in S}p(\hat{c}\mid S)\sum_{c}p(z\mid c,\hat{c},S)\,p(c\mid\hat{c},S), (33) where p ⁡ ( c ∣ c ^ , S ) p(c\mid\hat{c},S) is measured from Balrog , and p ⁡ ( z ∣ c , c ^ , S ) p(z\mid c,\hat{c},S) is calibrated from the redshift sample in the deep fields. In practice, we use the DES SOMPZ reweighting form, in which the Balrog distribution of deep cells is reweighted to match the deep-field population: p S ​ ( z ∣ c ^ ) ∝ ∑ c p ⁡ ( z ∣ c , c ^ , S ) ​ p B ​ ( c ∣ c ^ , S ) ​ p D ​ ( c ∣ S ) p B ​ ( c ∣ S ) . p_{S}(z\mid\hat{c})\propto\sum_{c}p(z\mid c,\hat{c},S)p_{\rm B}(c\mid\hat{c},S)\frac{p_{\rm D}(c\mid S)}{p_{\rm B}(c\mid S)}. (34) Here the subscripts B {\rm B} and D {\rm D} denote probabilities measured from Balrog and from the deep-field sample, respectively. The final redshift distribution for a sample is n S ​ ( z ) = ∑ c ^ ∈ S p W ​ ( c ^ ∣ S ) ​ p S ​ ( z ∣ c ^ ) , ∫ n S ​ ( z ) ​ 𝑑 z = 1 , n_{S}(z)=\sum_{\hat{c}\in S}p_{\rm W}(\hat{c}\mid S)\,p_{S}(z\mid\hat{c}),\qquad\int n_{S}(z)\,dz=1, (35) where p W ​ ( c ^ ∣ S ) p_{\rm W}(\hat{c}\mid S) is the weighted abundance of the selected wide-SOM cell in the fiducial Balrog catalog. The SOM maps in Fig. 4 summarize the mean redshift and sample-selection response to magnification across the 32 × 32 32\times 32 wide-cell grid. As seen there, the redshift structure is sufficiently smooth and well sampled for defining high- and low-redshift selections. The magnification response map shows that individual cell estimates are noisy, although an aggregate response can be measured with useful precision after many cells are combined. However, selecting extreme cells and evaluating their aggregate response with the same injections preferentially selects upward and downward noise fluctuations, and their true response variation should be estimated out of sample.

sections.heading: 3.3 High-redshift samples and direct evidence for response cancellation
sections.text: Figure 5: Redshift distributions and magnification responses of the SOM-selected DES Y6 samples. The top panel shows the SOMPZ redshift distributions for the full i < 27 i<27 parent sample, the union of the low-redshift lens bins, and the union of the high-redshift density bins, with the vertical dotted line marking the boundary used to isolate the high-redshift selections. The second panel shows the three low-redshift lens bins selected from the brighter i < 23 i<23 sample. The third panel shows the three high-redshift bins before splitting by magnification response. The bottom two panels show the same high-redshift bins after splitting wide SOM cells at C sample = 2 C_{\rm sample}=2 , giving branches with positive and negative net magnification response. Curves in the lower panels are normalized to unit peak for visual comparison. Legend entries report the number density of each sample and the measured C sample ± σ JK ​ ( C sample ) C_{\rm sample}\pm\sigma_{\rm JK}(C_{\rm sample}) , where the uncertainty is estimated from the spatial delete-one jackknife of the matched Balrog counts. The response values were evaluated using the same injection catalog used to assign cells to the branches, and so they are apparent in-sample estimates and should not be interpreted as unbiased estimates of the response separation achievable on an independent realization. We define each galaxy sample as a union of SOM cells. We separate the low-redshift lenses from the high-redshift position samples by requiring the redshift probability leaking across a boundary near z = 0.7 z=0.7 to be small. We adopt this boundary after visually inspecting the DES colour information and finding that the available filters provide particularly effective redshift discrimination around this value. Minimizing the overlap between the two redshift distributions is essential for suppressing the intrinsic galaxy-clustering signal from physically associated galaxies. We then subdivide the samples according to whether C sample c ^ C_{\rm sample}^{\hat{c}} lies above or below 2. The lens samples are built from the brighter magnitude threshold i < 23 i<23 . We first select low-redshift cells satisfying P ⁡ ( z < 0.60 ∣ c ^ ) > 0.98 P(z<0.60\mid\hat{c})>0.98 . These cells are then split into three lens bins using cumulative redshift-probability cuts: cells with P ⁡ ( z < 0.35 ∣ c ^ ) ≥ 0.80 P(z<0.35\mid\hat{c})\geq 0.80 , cells failing that condition but satisfying P ⁡ ( z < 0.45 ∣ c ^ ) ≥ 0.80 P(z<0.45\mid\hat{c})\geq 0.80 , and the remaining selected cells. This produces three low-redshift lens bins with increasing mean redshift. The high-redshift samples are built from a deeper selection without an additional magnitude threshold. We select cells for which P ⁡ ( z < 0.70 ∣ c ^ ) < 0.05 P(z<0.70\mid\hat{c})<0.05 , sort them by their SOMPZ mean redshift, and divide the ordered cells into three bins with approximately equal cumulative wide-cell abundance. These three parent samples form the basis for both the empirical response tests and the forecast samples below. Starting from the top, Figure 5 shows the corresponding redshift distributions, number counts, and measured values and corresponding errors of C sample C_{\rm sample} of the overall galaxy population, along with the low redshift and high redshift position samples we just described. The bottom two panels show versions of the high-redshift samples after splitting them on magnification response, which is described in § 3.3.2 .

sections.heading: 3.3.1 Magnitude partitions
sections.text: Figure 6: Measured sample-selection response for complementary magnitude partitions of the three DES Y6 high-redshift parent samples. The horizontal axis gives the fraction of the fiducial parent assigned to the brighter branch; the upper axis gives the corresponding i i -band threshold. Rose and blue curves show the responses of the bright and faint branches, respectively, and the dotted line marks C sample = 2 C_{\rm sample}=2 or C mag = 0 C_{\rm mag}=0 . Because the thresholds are defined by magnitude and sample fraction rather than by noisy per-cell response estimates, the figure provides direct evidence for response cancellation. At an illustrative 25/75 split, the bright/faint C mag C_{\rm mag} values are approximately ( + 1.21 , − 0.99 ) (+1.21,-0.99) , ( + 0.86 , − 1.39 ) (+0.86,-1.39) , and ( + 1.59 , + 0.01 ) (+1.59,+0.01) for high-redshift bins 1–3. The first two bins therefore contain substantial positive and negative contributions, while the third is predominantly positive. The shaded bands show the spatial jackknife uncertainty on each fixed magnitude selection. A direct and interpretable way to test for response cancellation is to partition each high-redshift parent sample at an observed i i -band magnitude threshold. For each chosen threshold i cut i_{\rm cut} , the bright and faint selections are complementary: H i bright = { g ∈ H i : i < i cut } , \displaystyle H_{i}^{\rm bright}=\{g\in H_{i}:i<i_{\rm cut}\}, (36) H i faint = { g ∈ H i : i ≥ i cut } . \displaystyle H_{i}^{\rm faint}=\{g\in H_{i}:i\geq i_{\rm cut}\}. (37) We choose thresholds corresponding to a predefined grid of fractions in the brighter branch and then measure the response of each complete branch using Eq. ( 27 ). Unlike the SOM-response split considered below, the membership of these branches is not determined by a noisy estimate of C sample C_{\rm sample} for each cell. The physical origin of the separation is simple. To first order, magnification changes an observed magnitude by δ ​ m ≃ − 5 ln ⁡ 10 ​ κ . \delta m\simeq-\frac{5}{\ln 10}\,\kappa. (38) Objects therefore move across an internal magnitude boundary: the brighter branch gains objects from the fainter branch, while the fainter branch loses them. When the two branches are recombined, this internal transfer cancels. The remaining response of the unsplit parent is set by its external detection and selection boundaries, as well as size, multiband signal-to-noise, photometric-redshift assignment, blending, and other measurement effects. The response of a simple flux-limited sample is governed by the local slope of the cumulative number counts; in these more complicated selections, the matched Balrog measurement propagates all of these effects jointly. Evolution of the luminosity function and selection boundaries with redshift can therefore produce two canceling branches in some tomographic bins but a mainly positive response in another. The magnitude partitions shown in Figure 6 establish that significant response separation is already available in a one-dimensional selection. They should not be regarded as the final optimized samples: the best selection may also use size, multiband fluxes, signal-to-noise, morphology, or other measured properties. They nevertheless demonstrate the physical cancellation that motivates BigMag without relying on the noisy ordering of individual SOM-cell responses. This is the photometric-galaxy analogue of the magnitude-dependent sign change observed in quasar and Lyman-break samples ( Scranton et al., 2005 ; Hildebrandt et al., 2009 ) , although here the response includes effects from the full selection. The 25/75 point in the caption is quoted as an illustrative common comparison across bins, not as a claim that this threshold maximizes cosmological information.

sections.heading: 3.3.2 SOM-response partitions
sections.text: The SOM provides a higher-dimensional route to response selection. Within each high-redshift parent bin, an exploratory split can be formed from the cell point estimates, H i + \displaystyle H_{i}^{\rm+} = { c ^ ∈ H i : C ^ sample ​ ( c ^ ) > 2 } , \displaystyle=\{\hat{c}\in H_{i}:\widehat{C}_{\rm sample}(\hat{c})>2\}, (39) H i − \displaystyle H_{i}^{\rm-} = { c ^ ∈ H i : C ^ sample ​ ( c ^ ) < 2 } . \displaystyle=\{\hat{c}\in H_{i}:\widehat{C}_{\rm sample}(\hat{c})<2\}. (40) When the same injection catalog is used to define and evaluate the branches, the H i + H_{i}^{+} and H i − H_{i}^{-} samples have positive and negative apparent net magnification responses, respectively, in the convention of Sec. 2.1 . Their redshift distributions, number counts, and all-injection estimates of C sample C_{\rm sample} and their jackknife uncertainties are shown in Fig. 5 . The split at C sample = 2 C_{\rm sample}=2 introduces a direct tradeoff between magnification response and number density. Cells with the most extreme values of C sample C_{\rm sample} provide the largest magnification signal per galaxy, but they occupy only a small fraction of the SOM and therefore yield low-density samples. Conversely, including cells progressively closer to C sample = 2 C_{\rm sample}=2 increases the number of galaxies, but reduces the net magnification response of the sample. The null-response partition used here is therefore a simple, physically motivated choice rather than a claim of optimality. An optimized selection could instead combine the SOM coordinates with magnitude, size, signal-to-noise, or other observed properties, and should maximize the expected cosmological information while propagating response and redshift-calibration uncertainty. The tests in Appendix A.1 and Appendix A.2 help distinguish between the presence of response cancellation and our ability to reliably identify the optimal response branches. In a DES-like Flagship sample, we recover the same qualitative trends with magnitude seen in the data: the first two high-redshift bins contain substantial positive and negative contributions, while the third is dominated by a positive response. When the number of galaxies per SOM cell is large, partitioning the sample by SOM response produces a strong and stable separation, with good agreement between in-sample and held-out measurements. However, once the Flagship sample is degraded to Balrog-like statistics, the contrast of the held-out responses is significantly reduced, closely resembling the behavior seen in DES. This shows that the SOM ordering does contain genuine information about the response, and that current DES injection statistics are not sufficient to fully optimize the partition of each tomographic bin by magnification response. Optimally separating each tomographic bin for magnification measurements requires a larger injection campaign with disjoint optimization and validation subsets. Appendix A.3 shows that the statistical uncertainty of the response follows the expected inverse-square-root scaling with the number of injections, supporting this strategy and quantifying the increase in injection statistics required for a precise calibration.

We assume the best-case scenario where all systematics have been corrected in all samples. We assume f sky = 0.12 f_{\rm sky}=0.12 , from DES, and include the relevant shot-noise and shape-noise contributions using the densities and ellipticity dispersions in Table 3.4 . For reference, we quote the raw signal-to-noise ratios of the simulated data-vector blocks over the full angular range used to generate the measurements, before applying any analysis scale cuts. Using all 27 angular bins between 1 1 and 500 500 arcmin, we find S / N ≃ 1254 S/N\simeq 1254 for the full galaxy-clustering block, S / N ≃ 484 S/N\simeq 484 for the full galaxy–galaxy lensing block, and S / N ≃ 165 S/N\simeq 165 for the cosmic-shear block. Figure 8 also shows two diagnostic comparison cases that are not included as separate observables in the fiducial likelihood: the cross-correlations using the unsplit high-redshift parent samples, and the same cross-correlations with the magnification response artificially set to zero. The simulated galaxy–galaxy lensing measurements are shown in Fig. 9 . The measurements naturally split into two redshift regimes. When the mean redshift of the position sample is lower than that of the source sample, the signal corresponds to traditional galaxy–galaxy lensing: the dominant contribution is the correlation between foreground galaxy density and background shear. This is the case for all low- z z lens–source combinations, L × \times S, shown in the left part of the figure. When the position sample is instead at higher redshift than the source sample, the standard density–shear contribution is suppressed and the measurement becomes an inverse galaxy–galaxy lensing (IGGL) signal, as defined in Sec. 2 and Cross and Sánchez (2024) . In this regime, the signal is sourced by the magnification contribution to the high-redshift position sample, and therefore changes sign between the positive- and negative-magnification selections. This is the dominant configuration for most H × \times S combinations shown in the right part of the figure. There are, however, mixed cases among the high-redshift lenses. This explains why this panel has the same qualitative sign for the positive- and negative-magnification selections, unlike the genuine IGGL configurations where the two selections trace opposite-sign signals. Separating the data vector into these two regimes, we find raw signal-to-noise ratios of S / N ≃ 470 S/N\simeq 470 for the traditional GGL subset and S / N ≃ 149 S/N\simeq 149 for the IGGL subset; the latter is comparable to the signal-to-noise of the simulated cosmic shear measurements, which are not shown because we will only use them for comparison/combination.

sections.heading: 4 Cosmological constraints from optimized magnification probes
sections.text: We now investigate the cosmological information carried by the optimized magnification observables introduced in the previous sections. We first consider the clustering-only BigMag data vector, isolating the role of the magnification-selected samples in breaking the degeneracy between galaxy bias and the amplitude of matter fluctuations, § 4.1 . We then study how its constraining power depends on the calibration of the magnification coefficients and compare it directly with traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt, § 4.2 , which provides a natural shear-based counterpart to BigMag. We subsequently add IGGL, study the complementarity between the two magnification probes, and compare their joint constraints with those from a traditional 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt analysis, § 4.3 . For each combination of observables, we compute theoretical predictions using CosmoSIS ( Zuntz et al., 2015b ) and evaluate a Gaussian likelihood, − 2 ​ ln ⁡ ℒ = ( 𝐝 − 𝐭 ⁡ ( ϑ ) ) T ​ 𝐂 − 1 ​ ( 𝐝 − 𝐭 ⁡ ( ϑ ) ) , -2\ln\mathcal{L}=\left(\mathbf{d}-\mathbf{t}(\boldsymbol{\vartheta})\right)^{\rm T}\mathbf{C}^{-1}\left(\mathbf{d}-\mathbf{t}(\boldsymbol{\vartheta})\right), (41) where 𝐝 \mathbf{d} is the simulated data vector described in Sec. 3.4 , 𝐭 ⁡ ( ϑ ) \mathbf{t}(\boldsymbol{\vartheta}) is its theoretical prediction, and 𝐂 \mathbf{C} is the fixed simulated covariance. sections.heading: 4.1 Clustering-only constraints: breaking the galaxy-bias degeneracy
sections.text: We begin with the clustering-only data vector, consisting of the autocorrelations of the three low-redshift lens samples and their cross-correlations with the high-redshift samples. As discussed in Sec. 2.2 , the amplitudes of these two classes of measurements can be written schematically, around the fiducial cosmology, as w L i ​ L i ​ ( θ ) \displaystyle w^{L_{i}L_{i}}(\theta) ∝ b i 2 ​ σ 8 2 ​ 𝒦 i δ ​ δ ​ ( θ , Ω m , … ) , \displaystyle\propto b_{i}^{2}\,\sigma_{8}^{2}\,\mathcal{K}^{\delta\delta}_{i}\left(\theta;\Omega_{\rm m},\ldots\right), (42) w L i ​ H j ​ ( θ ) \displaystyle w^{L_{i}H_{j}}(\theta) ∝ b i ​ C j mag ​ σ 8 2 ​ 𝒦 i ​ j δ ​ κ ​ ( θ , Ω m , … ) . \displaystyle\propto b_{i}\,C^{\rm mag}_{j}\,\sigma_{8}^{2}\,\mathcal{K}^{\delta\kappa}_{ij}\left(\theta;\Omega_{\rm m},\ldots\right). (43) Here 𝒦 δ ​ δ \mathcal{K}^{\delta\delta} and 𝒦 δ ​ κ \mathcal{K}^{\delta\kappa} represent the corresponding projection kernels and their residual dependence on cosmology after factoring out the dominant σ 8 2 \sigma_{8}^{2} scaling. In particular, they contain the dependence on Ω m \Omega_{\rm m} through the shape and evolution of the matter power spectrum, the distance–redshift relation, and, for 𝒦 δ ​ κ \mathcal{K}^{\delta\kappa} , the lensing-efficiency kernel. The two observables therefore have different dependences on both the nuisance parameters and cosmology. The low-redshift autocorrelations alone constrain approximately the combination b i ​ σ 8 b_{i}\sigma_{8} , modulated by their dependence on Ω m \Omega_{\rm m} and the remaining cosmological parameters. This produces the familiar degeneracy between galaxy bias and the amplitude of matter fluctuations. The magnification-dominated cross-correlations provide a second set of measurements, with a different dependence on b i b_{i} and on the cosmological kernels. If C j mag C^{\rm mag}_{j} is calibrated, jointly fitting the autocorrelations and cross-correlations can therefore separate the foreground galaxy biases from the cosmological lensing amplitude. We emphasize that the analysis does not construct or fit a ratio of these observables. The schematic scalings above only illustrate why the two sets of measurements contain complementary parameter dependences. In the inference, all autocorrelations and cross-correlations are fitted jointly, with their full covariance and their complete scale- and redshift-dependent theoretical predictions. The result is consequently a constraint on a combination of σ 8 \sigma_{8} and Ω m \Omega_{\rm m} , rather than on σ 8 \sigma_{8} alone. The BigMag and traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt posteriors follow somewhat different degeneracy directions in the Ω m \Omega_{\rm m} – σ 8 \sigma_{8} plane from that commonly found in cosmic-shear analyses. This is a common reference choice, rather than an exponent optimized for each posterior: the value that minimizes the marginalized uncertainty depends on the observables and magnification priors. Keeping the definition fixed ensures that all quoted improvements within these comparisons refer to the same parameter. The preferred exponent for each chain is reported separately in Table 3 . Contours show the 68 % 68\% and 95 % 95\% credible regions for the three low-redshift galaxy biases, Ω m \Omega_{\rm m} , σ 8 \sigma_{8} , and the derived parameter S 8 ′ = σ 8 ​ ( Ω m / 0.3 ) 0.7 S^{\prime}_{8}=\sigma_{8}(\Omega_{\rm m}/0.3)^{0.7} . Magnification in the unsplit samples provides only limited additional information because of cancellation between galaxies with opposite responses. The optimized split removes this cancellation, allowing the magnification-dominated cross-correlations to break the galaxy-bias degeneracy and constrain a combination of Ω m \Omega_{\rm m} and σ 8 \sigma_{8} . The remaining cross-correlation signal provides only limited leverage on the galaxy-bias degeneracy, leaving a broad constraint on S 8 ′ S^{\prime}_{8} . The result changes qualitatively for the optimized BigMag samples. Splitting each high-redshift sample into positive- and negative-response populations prevents this cancellation and produces high signal-to-noise cross-correlations with opposite signs. Thus, it is not merely the presence of magnification that enables clustering-only cosmological inference: selecting samples according to their magnification response is essential. This is one of the central results of this work. sections.heading: 4.2 Magnification calibration and comparison with traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt
sections.text: We next examine how uncertainty in the magnification coefficients affects the BigMag constraints and compare its limiting performance with that of a traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt analysis. The two analyses have analogous structures: both combine foreground galaxy clustering with a lensing-induced cross-correlation that helps separate galaxy bias from the amplitude of matter fluctuations. Traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt uses the cross-correlation between foreground positions and background galaxy shapes, whereas BigMag uses magnification-induced correlations between foreground and background galaxy positions. In both cases, the amplitude of the lensing observable depends on a response calibration. Galaxy–galaxy lensing depends on the multiplicative shear calibration factor 1 + m 1+m , while the BigMag cross-correlations depend linearly on C mag C^{\rm mag} . There is, however, an important physical difference between these parameters. The shear response remains close to unity and does not change the sign of the galaxy–galaxy lensing signal, whereas C mag C^{\rm mag} can be positive, negative, or close to zero. This sign dependence enables the sample optimization considered here: separating galaxies with positive and negative magnification responses prevents signal cancellation and produces cross-correlations with opposite signs. A further distinction concerns sensitivity to small scales. Tangential shear is non-local, so uncertainties below the minimum modeled scale propagate into the retained galaxy–galaxy lensing measurements. We mitigate this contribution by analytically marginalizing over an independent point-mass template for each retained position–source tomographic-bin pair ( MacCrann et al., 2020 ; Prat et al., 2022 ; Prat et al., 2023 ) . By contrast, BigMag traces convergence through magnification and has no analogous enclosed-mass contribution, although it remains subject to the usual nonlinear and baryonic modeling uncertainties on the retained scales. Having established these similarities and differences, we now quantify the role of magnification calibration. Our fiducial analysis adopts independent Gaussian priors with σ ⁡ ( C mag ) = 0.2 \sigma(C^{\rm mag})=0.2 , motivated by the calibration uncertainties obtained from the DES Y6+ Balrog measurements and sample selections described in Sec. 3 . Because C mag C^{\rm mag} controls the amplitude of each magnification cross-correlation, its uncertainty propagates directly into the inferred cosmological lensing amplitude. We therefore use Fig. 11 to examine how the constraints improve as the magnification calibration is made more precise. Tightening the magnification-coefficient priors from σ ⁡ ( C mag ) = 0.2 \sigma(C^{\rm mag})=0.2 to 0.1 0.1 reduces the half-width of the central 68 % 68\% credible interval on S 8 ′ S^{\prime}_{8} from 0.0434 0.0434 to 0.0278 0.0278 , an improvement of approximately 36 % 36\% , yielding S 8 ′ = 0.825 − 0.028 + 0.028 . S^{\prime}_{8}=0.825^{+0.028}_{-0.028}. (47) This result is obtained by importance-reweighting the fiducial BigMag chain. In the limiting case in which all magnification coefficients are fixed to their input values, the constraint becomes S 8 ′ = 0.827 − 0.018 + 0.018 , S^{\prime}_{8}=0.827^{+0.018}_{-0.018}, (48) with a credible-interval half-width of 0.0179 0.0179 , a factor of approximately 2.4 2.4 smaller than in the fiducial analysis. For comparison, the traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt analysis gives S 8 ′ = 0.824 − 0.015 + 0.015 , S^{\prime}_{8}=0.824^{+0.015}_{-0.015}, (49) with a half-width of 0.0153 0.0153 . Thus, the fixed-response BigMag uncertainty is approximately 17 % 17\% larger than that of the traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt analysis. All of these comparisons use the same fixed definition of S 8 ′ S^{\prime}_{8} with η = 0.7 \eta=0.7 , rather than separately optimized amplitude combinations. The reference 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt analysis adopts independent Gaussian shear-calibration priors with σ m = 0.01 \sigma_{m}=0.01 . The numerical widths of the m m and C mag C^{\rm mag} priors should not be compared directly because these parameters have different normalizations. The parameter m m describes a fractional multiplicative correction to the shear signal, whereas C mag C^{\rm mag} is the full magnification response. For the high-redshift split samples used here, | C mag | |C^{\rm mag}| ranges from 1.1 1.1 to 2.25 2.25 , so the fiducial prior width σ ⁡ ( C mag ) = 0.2 \sigma(C^{\rm mag})=0.2 corresponds to fractional response uncertainties of approximately 9 9 – 18 % 18\% . This interpretation does not apply to the low-redshift samples, whose fiducial magnification responses are zero. Moreover, the fixed- C mag C^{\rm mag} analysis assumes perfect magnification calibration, whereas the traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt analysis retains finite shear-calibration uncertainty. The comparison therefore demonstrates the limiting constraining power of BigMag under the adopted analysis choices, rather than performance under matched calibration uncertainties. Like the shear response, magnification coefficients can be calibrated empirically. Here, this calibration is provided by synthetic-source injections and the SOM-based methodology described in Sec. 3 . Increasing the number of injections and the calibration area, while improving the characterization of the relevant selection responses, could enable tighter magnification priors. We discuss this further in § 5.1 . These results demonstrate that, with sufficiently precise magnification calibration, magnification-selected clustering can approach the constraining power of traditional shear-based 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt analyses. Figure 11: Dependence of the BigMag cosmological constraints on the calibration of the magnification coefficients. Contours show the 68 % 68\% and 95 % 95\% credible regions in Ω m \Omega_{\rm m} , σ 8 \sigma_{8} , and S 8 ′ = σ 8 ​ ( Ω m / 0.3 ) 0.7 S^{\prime}_{8}=\sigma_{8}(\Omega_{\rm m}/0.3)^{0.7} . The dashed and dotted contours show BigMag with independent Gaussian magnification priors of σ ⁡ ( C mag ) = 0.2 \sigma(C^{\rm mag})=0.2 and 0.1 0.1 , respectively; the latter is obtained by importance-reweighting the fiducial chain. The dark-blue contours show the limiting case in which the magnification coefficients are fixed to their input values. For comparison, the red contours show a traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt analysis with Gaussian multiplicative shear-calibration priors of σ m = 0.01 \sigma_{m}=0.01 . Traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt combines lens clustering with shear-based galaxy–galaxy lensing, whereas BigMag combines lens clustering with magnification-induced position cross-correlations. All cases use the same fixed exponent η = 0.7 \eta=0.7 , allowing a direct comparison of their marginalized S 8 ′ S^{\prime}_{8} constraints. Tighter magnification calibration substantially improves the precision: with the magnification coefficients fixed, the central 68 % 68\% interval is approximately 17 % 17\% wider than for the reference traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt analysis, which retains finite shear-calibration uncertainty. Dashed grey lines indicate the input cosmology.

sections.heading: 4.4 Comparison and combination with traditional 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt
sections.text: Having established the complementarity of BigMag and IGGL, we now compare their joint cosmological constraints with those from traditional 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt and investigate the information gained by combining these observables. Traditional 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt combines foreground galaxy clustering, galaxy–galaxy lensing (the 2 × \times 2pt case from Sec. 4.2 ), and cosmic shear, and it represents the main weak lensing analysis for imaging surveys like DES ( DES Collaboration et al., 2026 ) . The combination of 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt with BigMag and IGGL contains the union of the traditional and magnification-based data vectors, with shared measurements counted once and their cross-covariance included. We retain the cosmological and nuisance-parameter treatment described above, including marginalization over galaxy bias, redshift uncertainties, shear calibration, intrinsic alignments, baryonic feedback, and point-mass contributions. We consider independent Gaussian magnification-response priors with widths σ C ≡ σ ⁡ ( C mag ) = 0.2 \sigma_{C}\equiv\sigma(C^{\rm mag})=0.2 and 0.02 0.02 , together with a broad uniform-prior case (flat C C ).
