sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: The forecasts presented in this work illustrate how magnification-selected position samples can recover lensing information lost when populations with opposite responses are combined. In the configuration adopted here, the high-redshift samples combine high number densities with substantial magnification responses. Their cross-correlations with foreground galaxies, together with foreground autocorrelations, allow BigMag to break the foreground galaxy-bias degeneracy, while the same samples provide a complementary IGGL signal. Combining BigMag and IGGL self-calibrates the magnification responses of the shared high-redshift samples and yields competitive constraints on the growth of structure. Under the adopted sample and calibration assumptions, BigMag can approach the amplitude precision of traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt, while BigMag+IGGL provides marginalized S 8 S_{8} constraints comparable to the traditional 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt reference, and tighter in the most precise magnification-calibration scenario considered here. These results motivate further development and validation of response-based galaxy selections. Realizing this potential in data will require establishing the achievable response contrast and number densities, independently calibrating the selected responses, and jointly characterizing their redshift dependence and the sample redshift distributions. Additional requirements include controlling intrinsic clustering from redshift overlap, mitigating observational effects in the foreground samples and those shared with the background samples, and validating the theoretical model on the scales included in the likelihood. In this section we discuss these requirements, the relation to previous magnification estimators, and possible extensions of BigMag.

sections.heading: 5.1 Calibration of the magnification response
sections.text: Realizing the full constraining power of the analysis requires an accurate absolute calibration of the magnification response of each high-redshift sample, but the observables themselves provide substantial internal calibration. Starting from broad, independent priors of σ ⁡ ( C mag ) = 0.2 \sigma(C_{\rm mag})=0.2 , BigMag reduces the marginalized response uncertainties to approximately 0.13 0.13 – 0.15 0.15 , while IGGL achieves 0.09 0.09 – 0.14 0.14 and their combination 0.06 0.06 – 0.12 0.12 (Fig. 12 ). Even with uniform priors on all responses, BigMag+IGGL yields a fractional precision on S 8 S_{8} of ≃ 1.6 % \simeq 1.6\% (Eq. 56 ), only ≃ 28 % \simeq 28\% larger than that of traditional 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt, while constraining the response uncertainties to ≃ 0.06 \simeq 0.06 – 0.18 0.18 . Imposing the fiducial σ C = 0.2 \sigma_{C}=0.2 priors then improves σ 68 ​ ( S 8 ) \sigma_{68}(S_{8}) by only ≃ 11 % \simeq 11\% . This self-calibration arises because each response coefficient must simultaneously describe multiple cross-correlations involving different foreground samples and lensing kernels, while the foreground autocorrelations constrain the galaxy biases entering the BigMag correlation functions. Self-calibration therefore mitigates, but does not eliminate, the need for accurate external response calibration: tightening the response priors substantially improves the cosmological constraints, and in the fixed-response limit the constraining power of BigMag becomes competitive with that of traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt for which we assume a 1 % 1\% relative uncertainty on the multiplicative shear calibration. Synthetic-source injections provide a direct route to this calibration by propagating a known magnification through detection, measurement, photometric-redshift assignment, and the final sample selection. Current publicly available injection campaigns, such as DES Y6 Balrog , achieve uncertainties of approximately σ ⁡ ( C mag ) ∼ 0.1 \sigma(C_{\rm mag})\sim 0.1 – 0.2 0.2 for the samples of this work. Appendix A.3 shows that this uncertainty follows the expected N inj − 1 / 2 N_{\rm inj}^{-1/2} scaling. Extrapolating this trend, a campaign covering the full DES footprint at 5 5 – 10 10 times the current injection density, and concentrating injections on the galaxies most likely to contribute to the high-redshift samples, would place the statistical response uncertainties close to ∼ 0.01 \sim 0.01 . The statistical precision assumed in the tight-prior forecasts therefore appears achievable with a larger, dedicated campaign. Defining the samples places a separate requirement on the injections. Because a sample response averages over many cells, individual cell responses are noisier than the aggregate by roughly the square root of the number of contributing cells. If the same noisy estimates are used both to assign cells to branches and to measure the branch responses, upward fluctuations are preferentially promoted into the positive-response branch and downward fluctuations into the negative-response branch, biasing the apparent contrast high even when each cell estimate is unbiased; this selection bias is not captured by the jackknife uncertainties of § 3.1 . Appendix A.2 shows that it is large for current DES statistics: on held-out injections, the branch contrast Δ ​ C ≡ C + mag − C − mag \Delta C\equiv C^{\rm mag}_{+}-C^{\rm mag}_{-} falls from ≃ 2.7 \simeq 2.7 – 3.5 3.5 to ≃ 0.9 \simeq 0.9 – 1.7 1.7 , with the positive-response branches consistent with the null response. Flagship reproduces this regression at Balrog-like per-cell noise, whereas at full statistics the in-sample and held-out responses agree and a contrast of Δ ​ C ≃ 1.6 \Delta C\simeq 1.6 survives, so the SOM carries genuine response information that current injections cannot fully exploit. Selections should therefore be defined and calibrated with disjoint injection subsets. The in-sample responses adopted in our forecasts (Table 3.4 ) should accordingly be read as targets, whose realization requires an injection campaign large enough both to select the branches reliably and to calibrate them, or an alternative method capable of robustly separating the branches. Increasing the number or area of injections reduces only the statistical component of the uncertainty. A precision analysis must also demonstrate that the injected population accurately represents the data across the joint space of colour, magnitude, size, morphology, and redshift. Because most current source-injection campaigns rely on empirical galaxy samples drawn from relatively small deep fields, additional strategies will be needed to quantify and mitigate the impact of sample variance in these reference populations, potentially using realistic models of galaxy populations ( Alarcon et al., 2026 ; Tortorelli et al., 2025 ; Thorp et al., 2025 , e.g.) . The systematic accuracy of the injection-based response measurement must also be established, in analogous work to that undertaken by the weak lensing shear community ( MacCrann et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Yoon et al., 2025 ; Yamamoto et al., 2025 ; Euclid Collaboration et al., 2025d ; Euclid Collaboration et al., 2025b ) . This includes testing the validity of the finite-difference approximation by comparing responses inferred from positive and negative magnifications, ± Δ ​ κ \pm\Delta\kappa , and, ideally, from several values of the applied convergence to identify any departures from linearity. In addition, potential residual dependencies of the inferred response on spatially varying observing conditions across the survey footprint should be quantified and, where necessary, incorporated into the calibration uncertainty budget. The response can also vary within a background tomographic bin ( Wenzl et al., 2024 , e.g.) . For a redshift distribution n i ​ ( z s ) n_{i}(z_{s}) normalized over source redshift and using χ s ≡ χ ⁡ ( z s ) \chi_{s}\equiv\chi(z_{s}) , this dependence enters through the response-weighted magnification kernel W mag , i ​ ( χ ) = 3 ​ Ω m ​ H 0 2 2 ​ c 2 ​ χ a ⁡ ( χ ) ​ ∫ z ⁡ ( χ ) ∞ d ​ z s ​ n i ​ ( z s ) ​ C mag , i ​ ( z s ) ​ χ s − χ χ s , W_{{\rm mag},i}(\chi)=\frac{3\Omega_{\rm m}H_{0}^{2}}{2c^{2}}\frac{\chi}{a(\chi)}\int_{z(\chi)}^{\infty}{\rm d}z_{s}\,n_{i}(z_{s})C_{{\rm mag},i}(z_{s})\frac{\chi_{s}-\chi}{\chi_{s}}, (60) such that δ g , i mag ​ ( 𝒏 ^ ) = ∫ d ​ χ ​ W mag , i ​ ( χ ) ​ δ m ​ ( χ ​ 𝒏 ^ , z ⁡ ( χ ) ) \delta_{g,i}^{\rm mag}(\hat{\boldsymbol{n}})=\int{\rm d}\chi\,W_{{\rm mag},i}(\chi)\delta_{\rm m}(\chi\hat{\boldsymbol{n}},z(\chi)) . Appendix D derives this result from the linear selection response of Sec. 2.1 and relates it to the sample-averaged response measured with synthetic-source injections. Consequently, the response entering a given cross-correlation is weighted by both the source distribution and the lensing geometry, and its effective value can differ among foreground kernels. Future analyses should therefore use source injections to characterize any redshift dependence of the magnification response and propagate the joint uncertainty in n i ​ ( z ) ​ C mag , i ​ ( z ) n_{i}(z)C_{{\rm mag},i}(z) , including the covariance between redshift and response calibration. The partial self-calibration supplied by BigMag and IGGL constrains effective response amplitudes, but cannot by itself protect against unmodeled redshift dependence or selection-response errors that are absorbed by those amplitudes.

sections.heading: 5.2 Redshift distributions and sample optimization
sections.text: Accurate redshift distributions are essential for interpreting the position-position correlations. For simplicity, our fiducial forecasts assign the positive- and negative-response branches of each high-redshift bin the same Gaussian n ⁡ ( z ) n(z) . The data-informed SOMPZ distributions shown in § 3.3 , however, reveal small differences between these branches, as well as extended low-redshift tails. A real-data analysis should use a separate redshift distribution for each selected sample and propagate its uncertainty jointly with that of the magnification response. The SOMPZ methodology used here provides a natural route to these branch-specific calibrations. The low-redshift tails deserve particular attention because galaxies that actually lie at the foreground redshift cluster physically with the lens sample, adding an intrinsic density-density contribution to the measured cross-correlation. On large scales, its amplitude depends on both the redshift overlap and the biases of the foreground and contaminating populations ( Garcia-Fernandez et al., 2018 ; Nicola et al., 2020 ) . For the three data-informed high-redshift samples, the fractions of their redshift distributions below z = 0.65 z=0.65 are approximately 0.010 0.010 , 0.015 0.015 , and 0.020 0.020 , with similar values for the positive- and negative-response branches. These numbers describe the total low-redshift tail, not the overlap with each individual lens bin. If the entire low-redshift tail were concentrated within the redshift range of a single lens bin, the resulting contamination would be localized to that cross-correlation; if instead the tail were spread across the full low-redshift range, the overlap with any one lens bin would be correspondingly smaller. Appendix B isolates this effect with a controlled experiment in which a fraction f overlap f_{\rm overlap} of each high-redshift distribution is replaced by the Gaussian distribution of a matched lens bin. Thus, f overlap f_{\rm overlap} represents a pair-specific contaminating component, rather than the total probability below z = 0.65 z=0.65 . For the scale cuts and covariance adopted here, f overlap = 0.01 f_{\rm overlap}=0.01 produces a density-only contribution with a signal-to-noise approximately 10 % 10\% of that of the magnification signal, with a roughly linear scaling at small overlap. The response split we have adopted here provides an important advantage in this respect, as selecting samples with larger | C mag | |C_{\rm mag}| strengthens the magnification contribution without producing a corresponding increase in the intrinsic density–density term. The BigMag selections therefore improve not only the magnification signal-to-noise, but also its contrast with physical-clustering contamination. Nevertheless, intrinsic clustering contributes positively to both response branches: as the overlap grows, it reinforces the positive-response correlation but suppresses, and can eventually reverse, the negative-response correlation. Residual overlap must therefore be modelled even when it remains subdominant in the total signal. These redshift-overlap considerations feed directly into the optimization of the response-selected samples. The split adopted here, at the null-response boundary ( C mag = 0 C_{\rm mag}=0 ), removes the leading cancellation between galaxies with opposite magnification responses and increases the contrast of magnification against intrinsic clustering. It does not, however, necessarily define the optimal selection. Moving toward more extreme response values can increase | C mag | |C_{\rm mag}| and make a fixed density-overlap contribution relatively less important, but it also reduces the galaxy number density and may select populations with less secure redshift distributions or response calibrations. Similarly, a denser parent sample can improve the trade-off between number density and magnification response, although deeper selections may also contain larger low-redshift tails. Future optimization should therefore maximize the expected marginalized cosmological information, rather than | C mag | |C_{\rm mag}| or the raw signal-to-noise alone, while accounting jointly for number density, response uncertainty, redshift overlap, contaminant galaxy bias, and sensitivity to observational systematics.

sections.heading: 5.3 Null-magnification samples
sections.text: A useful by-product of the framework developed here is the ability to construct samples that suppress magnification. Once the parent population has been characterized and divided according to its magnification response, the same information can be used both to select samples with large | C mag | |C_{\rm mag}| and to identify selections with C mag ≃ 0 C_{\rm mag}\simeq 0 . The latter could be obtained by selecting regions of galaxy-property space with small responses, or by combining opposite-response populations with suitable weights. Their construction therefore follows naturally from the calibration and sample-selection machinery already required for BigMag, without a separate calibration programme. Such samples would be useful for the galaxy-position component of traditional 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt analyses: suppressing their magnification response would reduce the additional contributions to galaxy clustering and galaxy–galaxy lensing while retaining the intrinsic clustering and its correlation with matter. This would simplify the interpretation of these observables and reduce their sensitivity to uncertainties in the magnification coefficients, whose importance has been demonstrated for current and future surveys ( Euclid Collaboration et al., 2022 ; Elvin-Poole et al., 2023 ) . The statistical benefit would depend on the number density, galaxy bias, and redshift distribution of the resulting selections, so a sample optimized for minimal magnification need not maximize the total cosmological information. Null-response lens samples would be particularly valuable for lensing-ratio measurements ( Jain and Taylor, 2003 ; Prat et al., 2019 ; Unruh et al., 2019 ; Sánchez et al., 2022 ; Emas et al., 2024 ; Giannini et al., 2026 ; Rana et al., 2026 ) . In the narrow-lens-bin limit, ratios of lensing signals measured around the same foreground galaxies can cancel the common dependence on galaxy bias and the galaxy–matter power spectrum, leaving ratios of lensing-distance factors. Magnification of the lens population introduces an additional correlation between foreground matter and the measured background lensing signal. This contribution involves a different line-of-sight kernel and does not generally cancel between the numerator and denominator, introducing dependence on the matter distribution and potentially on angular scale ( Unruh et al., 2019 ; Bermejo-Climent et al., 2020 ) . Selecting lenses with C mag ≃ 0 C_{\rm mag}\simeq 0 would suppress this contribution and help preserve the geometric interpretation that constitutes the main motivation behind these measurements. Realizing this benefit requires controlling the residual response across the lens redshift distribution, alongside the usual treatment of finite bin widths and other observational effects. Although optimizing and validating such samples is beyond the scope of this paper, the ability to construct both magnification-enhanced and near-null samples from the same calibrated parent population broadens the applications of the proposed selection framework.

sections.heading: 5.4 Observational systematics
sections.text: The BigMag background samples are dense and extend to faint galaxies close to the detection limit, making them particularly sensitive to spatial variations in observing conditions. As discussed in § 2.5 , this challenge is partly reduced because we do not use the autocorrelations of these samples, but only their cross-correlations with brighter foreground galaxies. The foreground samples retain the usual systematics requirements of a clustering analysis, since their autocorrelations enter the data vector directly. Once the foreground density field has been properly corrected, fluctuations affecting only the background selection do not bias the mean cross-correlation, provided that they are uncorrelated with the corrected foreground field. They can nevertheless increase the covariance and reduce the achievable signal-to-noise. Shared or correlated residual systematics can still bias the measurement. In an optimal analysis both samples should be carefully characterized and corrected, following the systematics-mitigation strategies developed for modern clustering analyses using survey-property maps of depth, seeing, extinction or stellar density ( Weaverdyck and Huterer, 2021 ; Berlfein et al., 2024 ; Rodríguez-Monroy et al., 2025 ; Sánchez et al., 2023 ) . Observing conditions can also change the composition of a selected sample across the footprint, producing spatial variations in its redshift distribution, galaxy bias, or magnification response. These subsample effects should be propagated into the theoretical prediction or corrected, since otherwise they may bias the inferred cosmological signal ( Kong et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 , e.g.) . A real-data analysis must additionally test whether the background selection is independent of the foreground density itself. This assumption can fail through effects local to the foreground galaxies, including blending and deblending failures, local background-subtraction errors, and dust extinction, obscuration or chromatic effects induced by nearby galaxies or intracluster light from the foreground sample. Such effects can generate foreground–background correlations even after large-scale observing conditions have been corrected. They have previously been investigated in flux-magnification analyses ( Ménard et al., 2010 ; Hildebrandt, 2016 ; Gaztanaga et al., 2021 ) , and their impact on observed number counts can be further characterized and mitigated using image-level source-injection campaigns such as Balrog .

sections.heading: 5.5 Theoretical modeling, foreground magnification and small-scale extensions
sections.text: The forecasted constraining power depends on the adopted nonlinear model and scale cuts. We use a minimum transverse separation of 4 ​ h − 1 ​ Mpc 4\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc} for the clustering measurements entering BigMag and for traditional galaxy-galaxy lensing. As shown in § 4.1 , adding a second-order galaxy-bias parameter produces only a small loss of precision, which is encouraging, but does not by itself demonstrate that the model will remain unbiased when applied to data. A real data analysis should validate the scale cuts using realistic simulations or contaminated synthetic data, including scale-dependent galaxy bias or baryonic effects absent from the fiducial model. The adopted choices should only be accepted after showing that they recover unbiased cosmological constraints, following tests similar to those developed in usual lensing analyses ( Sanchez-Cid et al., 2026 , e.g.) . The position-position magnification signal has a different radial dependence from traditional galaxy–galaxy lensing. Schematically, γ t ​ ( R ) \displaystyle\gamma_{\rm t}(R) ∝ Δ ​ Σ ​ ( R ) = Σ ¯ ( < R ) − Σ ⁡ ( R ) , \displaystyle\propto\Delta\Sigma(R)=\overline{\Sigma}(<R)-\Sigma(R), (61) w g ​ μ ​ ( R ) \displaystyle w_{g\mu}(R) ∝ Σ ⁡ ( R ) , \displaystyle\propto\Sigma(R), (62) up to the corresponding redshift kernels and response factors. The galaxy-galaxy lensing signal at a retained separation therefore depends on the matter distribution at all smaller separations. As discussed in § 4.2 , uncertainty in the mass below the minimum modeled scale can leak into the retained measurements and is commonly mitigated through point-mass marginalization or an equivalent localization procedure ( MacCrann et al., 2020 ; Prat et al., 2023 ) . The leading BigMag signal does not contain this same enclosed-mass contribution, so its scale cut acts more locally in projected separation. This does not make BigMag insensitive to nonlinear physics on the retained scales, but it may make the separation between modeled and excluded scales cleaner than in traditional galaxy-galaxy lensing. In our forecasts we conservatively apply point-mass marginalization to every retained position-shear correlation, including those dominated by IGGL. The dominant IGGL contribution, ⟨ κ ​ γ ⟩ \langle\kappa\gamma\rangle , and the residual traditional-lensing contribution, ⟨ δ g ​ γ ⟩ \langle\delta_{g}\gamma\rangle , have different physical kernels, so the nuisance treatment inherited from traditional galaxy-galaxy lensing might be conservative or at least non-optimal. A future analysis could model these terms separately and associate unresolved-scale nuisance parameters only with the contributions that require them, after validating the procedure with simulations. We have also simplified the forecasts by setting the magnification response of the foreground samples to zero. In real data this response will generally be nonzero, introducing additional density-magnification terms in the foreground autocorrelations and a smaller ⟨ κ ​ κ ⟩ \langle\kappa\kappa\rangle contribution to the foreground–background cross-correlations. These terms should be included in the model and may themselves carry useful cosmological information, although the magnification contribution to clustering autocorrelations is small compared to intrinsic clustering. The different and more local projected-scale dependence of BigMag also makes it an interesting probe of the galaxy-halo connection on smaller scales ( Wechsler and Tinker, 2018 ) . A more complete small-scale analysis could combine BigMag with galaxy-galaxy lensing and clustering using halo models ( Zacharegkas et al., 2025 ; Dvornik et al., 2023 ; Chaurasiya et al., 2024 ) , subhalo abundance matching ( Mahony et al., 2026 ) , or differentiable galaxy–halo models based on parametrized physical prescriptions for galaxy star formation history ( Hearin et al., 2021 ; Alarcon et al., 2023 ; Alarcon et al., 2026 ) and stellar population synthesis ( Hearin et al., 2023 ) . The complementary radial weighting of these observables could help separate galaxy-halo physics from cosmology. Exploiting this information will require accurate modeling of nonlinear bias, baryonic effects, higher-order magnification, and the covariance with the large-scale data vector. Complementing these model-dependent small-scale extensions, Appendix C considers a more agnostic use of the excluded BigMag measurements through magnification ratios. These ratios partially cancel the unknown small-scale galaxy–matter correlation while retaining information about relative magnification responses and, when different source redshifts are compared, lensing geometry, similarly to conventional lensing ratios ( Prat et al., 2019 ) . For the positive- and negative-response branches of the same tomographic bin, the common foreground mass profile cancels to leading order, such that their correlation ratio directly constrains C mag − / C mag + C_{\rm mag}^{-}/C_{\rm mag}^{+} and hence the anti-correlated combination of the two responses. However, a common rescaling of both coefficients leaves this ratio unchanged and can be absorbed by the BigMag lensing amplitude, yielding little improvement in the cosmological constraints. Ratios across source-redshift bins additionally retain a lensing-efficiency ratio, although this geometric information is weak for our sample configuration and remains degenerate with response and redshift-distribution uncertainties. These measurements can therefore provide useful internal calibration and consistency tests, but they do not determine the absolute response normalization nor add significant cosmological information for the configuration considered here.

sections.heading: 5.6 Relation to previous magnification estimators
sections.text: The analysis presented here builds on a broad literature investigating magnification as both a cosmological signal and a contribution to standard large-scale-structure observables. Early studies developed quasar–galaxy density correlations and related higher-order statistics ( Ménard and Bartelmann, 2002 ; Ménard et al., 2003 ) . They showed that, because faint sources with C mag < 0 C_{\rm mag}<0 are anti-correlated with foreground mass, an unweighted sample can suppress or even reverse the signal. It also derived optimal weights under which every magnitude bin contributes constructively. Subsequent work examined the complementarity of number-count magnification with shear ( van Waerbeke, 2010 ; Duncan et al., 2014 ) and of size magnification with shape ( Heavens et al., 2013 ) ; its effects on source counts and fluxes ( Jain and Lima, 2011 ) ; and estimators that null, remove or cancel the intrinsic clustering signal ( Zhang and Pen, 2005 ; Zhang and Pen, 2006 ; Heavens and Joachimi, 2011 ; Hou et al., 2021 ; Ma et al., 2024 ) . The sensitivity of inverse galaxy–galaxy lensing to magnification has also been explored ( Liu et al., 2021 ; Cross and Sánchez, 2024 ) . In the context of modern surveys, several studies have shown that neglecting magnification can bias clustering, lensing, and 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt analyses ( Duncan et al., 2014 ; Cardona et al., 2016 ; Villa et al., 2018 ; Lorenz et al., 2018 ; Thiele et al., 2020 ; Deshpande et al., 2020 ; Unruh et al., 2020 ; Duncan et al., 2022 ; Euclid Collaboration et al., 2022 ; Euclid Collaboration et al., 2024 ) , while recent work has assessed its additional constraining power in LSST-like and submillimetre surveys ( Mahony et al., 2022 ; Cueli et al., 2025 ; Bonavera et al., 2025 ) . Together, these studies establish both the need to model magnification accurately and its potential value as a deliberately constructed cosmological observable. The measurements most closely related to BigMag use magnification bias in galaxy number density. In this approach, foreground positions are correlated with the angular density of a more distant population, producing a position–position lensing statistic when the samples have negligible redshift overlap. Such measurements have been performed using quasars ( Gaztañaga, 2003 ; Myers et al., 2005 ; Scranton et al., 2005 ) , Lyman-break galaxies ( Hildebrandt et al., 2009 ; Morrison et al., 2012 ) , and photometrically selected galaxy samples ( Garcia-Fernandez et al., 2018 ; Nicola et al., 2020 ) . Several of these analyses measured the correlation in magnitude bins, observed the sign change predicted by C mag C_{\rm mag} between bright and faint sources, and combined bins with weights ( Scranton et al., 2005 ; Hildebrandt et al., 2009 ; Morrison et al., 2012 ; Garcia-Fernandez et al., 2018 ) . A sustained line of work has used high-redshift submillimetre galaxies, whose steep number counts and strong redshift separation can produce a large magnification-bias signal ( Lima et al., 2010 ; Wang et al., 2011 ; Hildebrandt et al., 2013 ; González-Nuevo et al., 2014 ; González-Nuevo et al., 2017 ; González-Nuevo et al., 2021 ; González-Nuevo et al., 2026 ; Bonavera et al., 2019 ; Bonavera et al., 2020 ; Bonavera et al., 2021 ; Bonavera et al., 2024 ; Cueli et al., 2021 ; Cueli et al., 2022 ; Cueli et al., 2024 ; Crespo et al., 2022 ; Fernandez-Fernandez et al., 2025 ) . These applications range from cross-correlation detections and tomography to constraints on cosmology, halo models, and the halo mass function. Related count-based measurements have used magnification bias as a mass probe for galaxy groups and clusters ( Van Waerbeke et al., 2010 ; Hildebrandt et al., 2011 ; Ford et al., 2012 ; Umetsu, 2013 ; Coupon et al., 2013 ; Ford et al., 2014 ; Chiu et al., 2016 ; Chiu et al., 2020 ; Tudorica et al., 2017 ; Murray et al., 2025 ) . Flux-dependent combinations of galaxy-count maps have also been used to reconstruct convergence from DECaLS and DES Y3 data by cancelling deterministic galaxy bias ( Qin et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2025b ; Qin et al., 2025a ) . These methods demonstrate the range of information available from source counts, but also emphasize their sensitivity to the response of the selected population and to contaminants such as redshift overlap, dust, blending, and obscuration. Other estimators use lensing-induced changes in galaxy flux, magnitude, or size more directly, with the unlensed reference supplied by a population distribution or an empirical scaling relation. Applications include correlated shifts in ensemble observables ( Ménard et al., 2010 ; Schmidt et al., 2012 ; Bauer et al., 2014 ; Xu et al., 2024 ) , Fundamental-Plane residuals used as noisy galaxy-level convergence proxies ( Bertin and Lombardi, 2006 ; Sonnenfeld et al., 2011 ; Huff and Graves, 2014 ; Freudenburg et al., 2020 ) , and Bayesian convergence likelihoods based on the joint intrinsic distribution of galaxy size, magnitude, and redshift ( Alsing et al., 2015 ) . A related population-inference principle underlies Bayesian Fourier Domain methods, which operate on PSF-corrected image moments and could in principle infer magnification jointly with shear, although published demonstrations have focused on shear ( Bernstein and Armstrong, 2014 ; Bernstein et al., 2016 ) . These direct estimators require careful calibration of the unlensed population and control of photometric noise, dust, blending, obscuration, and selection effects ( Hildebrandt, 2016 ; Gaztanaga et al., 2021 ) . Fundamental-Plane residuals present the additional complication that they correlate intrinsically with large-scale environment and can therefore mimic lensing ( Joachimi et al., 2015 ) . BigMag belongs to the established class of position–position magnification estimators. It shares with the C mag C_{\rm mag} -weighted estimators and flux-bin estimators mentioned before the principle that sources with opposite responses should not be combined with a common sign. It differs from them in three respects. First, the response of each candidate selection is calibrated end-to-end with image-level injections, which include detection, size, blending and SOM/photometric-redshift assignment, rather than being inferred from how the luminosity function translates into an α ⁡ ( m ) \alpha(m) relation. Second, these same calibrated responses are used to define the background samples in multi-dimensional color-magnitude space using the SOM. Third, the resulting branches enter as separate tracers in a joint likelihood with foreground clustering and with IGGL, rather than being compressed into a single weighted correlation or convergence map. Keeping these populations separate recovers signal that would otherwise be lost through cancellation and provides internal tests using positive, negative, and near-zero-response samples. In addition, the different positive and negative branches trace a common nuisance field, the intrinsic clustering density field of the background sources, acting as a sort of multi-tracer field included through the joint covariance. This is the principle behind flux-bin magnification reconstructions ( Zhang and Pen, 2005 ; Qin et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2025b ; Qin et al., 2025a ) , and is closely related to multi-tracer cancellation of sample variance ( Seljak, 2009 ) . A natural extension of BigMag would be to use the same background populations to construct a complementary flux-magnification observable by cross-correlating foreground galaxy positions with fluctuations in the mean flux or magnitude of the background galaxies ( Ménard et al., 2010 ; Jain and Lima, 2011 ; Bauer et al., 2014 ) . With negligible redshift overlap, this observable depends on the same foreground galaxy bias and matter–convergence correlation as the position-position magnification signal, but its amplitude is set by a distinct flux-response coefficient. The effective response of the measured ensemble flux, including the effects of detection, measurement noise, blending, non-detections, and sample selection, could in principle be calibrated using the same matched magnified and unmagnified synthetic-source injections employed for the number-density response ( Hildebrandt, 2016 ; Elvin-Poole et al., 2023 ; Anbajagane et al., 2025 ; Legnani et al., 2026 ) . The samples optimized for number-density magnification need not be optimal for the flux observable, but their joint analysis could recover additional information and provide further consistency tests. Such an analysis would require careful treatment of dust extinction, obscuration, blending, and spatial photometric-calibration errors ( Ménard et al., 2010 ; Hildebrandt et al., 2013 ; Hildebrandt, 2016 ; Gaztanaga et al., 2021 ) . Multi-band flux and colour information could help separate these effects because gravitational magnification is achromatic, whereas dust extinction is generally wavelength dependent. We leave the development of this joint number-density and flux-magnification analysis to future work.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we have developed an injection-calibrated strategy for selecting galaxy subpopulations according to their magnification response, using observed photometric properties and self-organizing maps. We call the resulting position-only analogue of a traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt analysis BigMag: it combines the autocorrelations of foreground position samples with lensing-dominated position–position cross-correlations between foreground and background galaxies. We assessed its cosmological potential using DES-informed redshift distributions and number densities together with simulated data vectors. The cosmological forecasts adopt a possible but optimistic response-separation scenario motivated by the DES measurements and by the Flagship validation tests. Our main conclusions are: • BigMag extracts weak-lensing information using galaxy positions alone. Separating background galaxies with different magnification responses prevents positive and negative contributions to the foreground–background cross-correlations from cancelling. Combining these cross-correlations with foreground galaxy clustering helps break the degeneracy between foreground galaxy bias and the amplitude of matter fluctuations. • Using DES Year 6 photometry, SOMPZ redshift calibration, and Balrog synthetic-source injections, we constructed dense high-redshift candidate samples and found direct evidence for substantial magnification-response cancellation. Complementary magnitude partitions produce order-unity response differences, with positive- and negative-response populations in the first two high-redshift bins and a predominantly positive response in the third. Validation and simulation tests show, however, that the current Balrog statistics are insufficient to optimally achieve the full magnification response separation in the data with a SOM. DES-like Flagship simulations demonstrate that a SOM partition can recover a large and stable held-out separation when the per-cell responses are measured with sufficiently high signal-to-noise. • In the adopted response-separation scenario, splitting the background samples increases the raw signal-to-noise of the foreground–background position cross-correlations, before analysis scale cuts, from approximately 64 to 194. The resulting correlations break the foreground-bias–matter-amplitude degeneracy. When the magnification coefficients are fixed, the marginalized S 8 ′ S^{\prime}_{8} uncertainty from BigMag is approximately 17 % 17\% larger than that from the reference traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt analysis, which retains its fiducial small shear-calibration uncertainty. • The same response-selected position samples generate a high signal-to-noise inverse galaxy-galaxy lensing (IGGL) observable with complementary dependencies on cosmology and nuisance parameters. Combining BigMag and IGGL reduces the marginalized uncertainties on the six high-redshift magnification responses from prior widths of 0.2 0.2 to approximately 0.055 0.055 – 0.12 0.12 . With the fiducial response priors, their joint analysis yields σ 68 ​ ( S 8 ) = 0.0117 \sigma_{68}(S_{8})=0.0117 , approximately 15 % 15\% larger than the traditional 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt reference. For σ ⁡ ( C mag ) = 0.02 \sigma(C_{\rm mag})=0.02 , the joint magnification constraint becomes approximately 14 % 14\% tighter than that reference. • Adding BigMag and IGGL to traditional 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt reduces the forecast S 8 S_{8} uncertainty by approximately 16 % 16\% for the fiducial response priors and by 29 % 29\% for σ ⁡ ( C mag ) = 0.02 \sigma(C_{\rm mag})=0.02 . These gains are conditional on the adopted response amplitudes and modeling assumptions. Realizing them in data will require independently validated magnification responses, accurate redshift calibration, control of redshift overlap and shared observational systematics, and validated nonlinear modeling. The measured injection-statistics scaling from Appendix A.3 suggests that statistical response uncertainties near 0.01 0.01 could be reached with a full-footprint injection campaign at approximately 5 5 – 10 10 times the current injection density, although systematic calibration uncertainties must be controlled separately. • The results in this paper motivate further development and validation of galaxy selections that maximize the cosmological information available from magnification. Applying the strategies explored here, and investigating alternative selections and galaxy populations, will establish the performance achievable in real data. The resulting samples can then be used to constrain cosmology through BigMag and IGGL, both jointly and in combination with traditional 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt analyses. The same framework can also be used to construct samples with near-zero magnification response, suppressing lens-magnification contributions to traditional 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt analyses and helping preserve the geometric interpretation of lensing-ratio measurements.

sections.heading: Statement on AI use
sections.text: Most of the central ideas underlying this paper were developed approximately a year ago, without the use of LLMs, through consideration of the physics of magnification and exploratory work with the publicly available Balrog products. This led to the preparation of the configuration files used to run the inference chains with CosmoSIS in successive stages, with only minimal assistance from LLMs. After the main results had been obtained, Codex was used more extensively to accelerate the production of plots, which were subsequently reviewed and manually edited. Codex was also used to assist with drafting and editing portions of the manuscript, as well as with the full implementation and partial drafting of the four appendices. Claude was additionally used to provide referee-style feedback on the manuscript. Both Claude and Codex were also used to comment on whether literature citations appropriately supported the corresponding statements and as search tools to identify related ideas and approaches in the literature. Any references identified in this way were subsequently checked manually, and, to the best of our ability, all citations in the manuscript were reviewed without relying solely on information provided by LLMs. In the interest of full disclosure, this paragraph was itself edited with the assistance of Codex.

sections.heading: A.1 DES Y6-like sample in Flagship
sections.text: To aid the interpretation of the trends measured in DES Y6, we construct a DES-like galaxy sample from the Flagship simulation ( Euclid Collaboration et al., 2025a ) . Flagship provides noiseless attenuated DECam g ​ r ​ i ​ z griz fluxes, but not a corresponding DES noise model. We therefore use the band-matched LSST flux uncertainties and noise realizations supplied with Flagship, scaling both by a factor of four to approximate the depth of the DES measurements. The fiducial observed flux in each band is constructed by adding this scaled noise realization to the DECam flux. For the magnified realization, we multiply the noiseless flux by μ = ( 1 − Δ ​ κ ) − 2 \mu=(1-\Delta\kappa)^{-2} , with Δ ​ κ = 0.01 \Delta\kappa=0.01 , before adding the same noise realization. Keeping the noise fixed ensures that changes in sample membership are produced by the applied magnification rather than by a second noise draw. Our parent catalog is the union of galaxies that satisfy an observed i i -band signal-to-noise threshold of five in either the fiducial or magnified realization. Including objects selected only after magnification is essential: otherwise, the response from galaxies entering the catalog through the detection boundary would be omitted. We train a 32 × 32 32\times 32 SOM using the fiducial g ​ r ​ i ​ z griz photometry and its uncertainties, and apply the same trained map to the fiducial and magnified realizations. Their matched count difference then gives C sample C_{\rm sample} through Eq. ( 27 ). This is a catalog-level validation rather than a fully image-level simulation: it captures the photometric selection and SOM reassignment caused by magnification, but not all of the blending and measurement effects present in the DES Balrog analysis. Figure 15 shows how the mean redshift and C sample C_{\rm sample} vary across the Flagship SOM. As in the data, the SOM organizes galaxies into extended regions with smoothly varying redshift, while the response contains additional structure within and across those regions. Cells at similar mean redshift can therefore have substantially different magnification responses. This is the behavior needed for the SOM to provide a higher-dimensional response selection rather than acting only as a redshift estimator. The lower panel shows the corresponding sample response C sample C_{\rm sample} , measured by comparing the matched fiducial and Δ ​ κ = 0.01 \Delta\kappa=0.01 realizations. The response map uses all Flagship SOM assignments available for this analysis. The null magnification-selection response is C sample = 2 C_{\rm sample}=2 . We form three high-redshift samples using the same cell-based construction as for the DES selections. We first retain cells for which less than five per cent of the assigned population lies below z = 0.7 z=0.7 . We then order the retained cells by their mean redshift and divide them into three approximately equipopulated bins. Their normalized redshift distributions are shown in Fig. 16 . The bins have mean redshifts of approximately 0.92 0.92 , 1.07 1.07 , and 1.25 1.25 , and reproduce the broad ordering and overlap of the DES high-redshift samples sufficiently well for the qualitative tests below. Differences in the detailed redshift distributions and number densities mean that the comparison should not be interpreted as a precise simulation-based prediction for DES. The vertical dashed line marks z = 0.7 z=0.7 . As a first test of response cancellation, we repeat the complementary magnitude partitions used for the DES data in Fig. 6 . For every threshold, the brighter and fainter branches form an exhaustive partition of the parent tomographic sample. Magnification moves galaxies through their common magnitude boundary, increasing the abundance of one branch while decreasing that of the other. This internal transfer cancels when the two branches are recombined, so a small response of the parent sample can conceal two substantially larger and oppositely signed contributions. Figure 17 shows that the Flagship samples display the same qualitative behavior as the data. At the illustrative 25/75 bright/faint split, the Flagship branch responses in C mag C_{\rm mag} units are approximately ( + 1.32 , − 0.41 ) (+1.32,-0.41) , ( + 1.02 , − 0.60 ) (+1.02,-0.60) , and ( + 2.01 , + 0.76 ) (+2.01,+0.76) for bins 1–3, respectively. The precise amplitudes differ from those measured in DES, as expected from the differences in photometry, redshift distributions, number densities, and measurement model. Nevertheless, both data sets exhibit order-unity branch responses: the first two bins contain clear cancellation between positive- and negative-response populations, while the response of the third bin is predominantly positive. The agreement in these broad trends supports the physical interpretation of the DES magnitude partitions and establishes that significant response separation is possible without selecting on noisy per-cell response estimates. The horizontal axis gives the fraction of the fiducial parent sample in the brighter branch; the upper axis gives the corresponding i i -band threshold. sections.heading: A.2 Held-out validation of magnification response
sections.text: The magnitude-partition test demonstrates that the parent samples contain populations with different responses, but it does not establish how accurately those populations can be identified from the current SOM-cell response estimates. If the same finite injection sample is used both to rank cells and to evaluate the resulting branches, statistical fluctuations preferentially promote cells with upward fluctuations into the higher-response branch and cells with downward fluctuations into the lower-response branch. The apparent contrast is then biased high by this selection, even when the response estimate of every individual cell is unbiased before selection. We test this effect with a held-out construction. For the DES Y6 Balrog catalogs, we divide the parent deep-galaxy IDs into two independent halves, keeping all repeated injections of a given deep object in the same half. One half is used to estimate the response of each SOM cell and to define branches with C ^ cell > 2 \widehat{C}_{\rm cell}>2 and C ^ cell < 2 \widehat{C}_{\rm cell}<2 . The aggregate responses of these fixed branches are then evaluated using only the other half. We repeat the procedure over 20 random divisions and exchange the roles of the two halves. The Flagship tests use the analogous train/held-out split of the matched simulated galaxies. Figure 18 compares the resulting in-sample and held-out measurements. In the DES panel, the held-out branch contrast is substantially smaller than the in-sample contrast. The response ordering still contains predictive information, but the current Balrog statistics are insufficient to validate the full apparent separation obtained when the same injections are used for both cell selection and response measurement. The middle panel repeats the test after reducing the Flagship catalog to one per cent of the eventual simulated sample, chosen to give a Balrog-like per-cell noise level. It exhibits the same regression of the held-out values toward the null response, demonstrating that finite per-cell statistics alone can reproduce the qualitative behavior seen in the data. The right panel instead uses the maximum available Flagship sample. In this high-statistics limit, the in-sample and held-out measurements agree closely in all three tomographic bins, and the fixed SOM split recovers a large response contrast on unseen galaxies. The comparison between the middle and right panels is particularly informative: both use the same underlying galaxy population and SOM, and differ primarily in the number of objects available to calibrate each cell. The reduction seen in the middle panel is therefore not evidence that the SOM variables lack response information; it is the expected winner’s-curse effect from optimizing on noisy cell estimates. Figure 18: Held-out validation of SOM-cell response selections in DES Y6 and the DES-like Flagship sample. Filled circles and solid lines show in-sample responses for branches selected above (red) and below (blue) the estimated cell-level null response. Open squares and dashed lines show the responses obtained when the cells are selected using one half of the objects and the fixed branches are evaluated using the independent half. The left panel shows the DES Y6 Balrog result, with error bars giving the scatter across the held-out realizations. The middle panel shows Flagship after culling it to approximately one per cent of the eventual catalog, producing a Balrog-like per-cell noise level. The right panel uses the maximum available Flagship sample. The contraction of the held-out contrast at low statistics, and its disappearance in the high-statistics Flagship result, isolate the selection bias caused by noisy per-cell response estimates. Based on these tests, the current SOM-selected DES branches identify promising directions in galaxy-property space, but their in-sample amplitudes should be regarded as optimistic targets rather than as independently validated response calibrations. At the same time, the magnitude partitions establish directly in the data that substantial cancellation is present, and the high-statistics Flagship test shows that a SOM-based selection can recover a strong and stable held-out separation once the cell responses are measured precisely. A larger image-injection campaign, with disjoint optimization and validation samples, is therefore the natural route to determining how much of this potential can be realized in DES-like data or in future surveys. The following subsection quantifies how the statistical precision of the response calibration scales with the size of such an injection campaign.

sections.heading: A.3.1 Origin of the inverse-square-root scaling
sections.text: The inverse-square-root scaling can be understood using an idealized Bernoulli model in which all injection attempts share the same selection probabilities within the fiducial/magnified campaigns, and different attempts are statistically independent. Consider n n independent injection attempts and let p 0 p_{0} and p κ p_{\kappa} be the probabilities that an injected object enters the sample in the fiducial and magnified runs. If the two selection indicators for a paired attempt have covariance c c , then Var ⁡ ( p ^ r ) = p r ​ ( 1 − p r ) / n \operatorname{Var}(\widehat{p}_{r})=p_{r}(1-p_{r})/n and Cov ⁡ ( p ^ κ , p ^ 0 ) = c / n \operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{p}_{\kappa},\widehat{p}_{0})=c/n . Expanding the estimator C ^ sample = p ^ κ − p ^ 0 p ^ 0 ​ Δ ​ κ \widehat{C}_{\rm sample}=\frac{\widehat{p}_{\kappa}-\widehat{p}_{0}}{\widehat{p}_{0}\,\Delta\kappa} (66) to first order in the fluctuations of p ^ 0 \widehat{p}_{0} and p ^ κ \widehat{p}_{\kappa} about their expectation values, and propagating their variances and covariance, gives Var ⁡ ( C ^ sample ) ≃ 1 n ​ Δ ​ κ 2 ​ [ p κ ​ ( 1 − p κ ) p 0 2 + p κ 2 ​ ( 1 − p 0 ) p 0 3 − 2 ​ p κ ​ c p 0 3 ] . \operatorname{Var}(\widehat{C}_{\rm sample})\simeq\frac{1}{n\,\Delta\kappa^{2}}\left[\frac{p_{\kappa}(1-p_{\kappa})}{p_{0}^{2}}+\frac{p_{\kappa}^{2}(1-p_{0})}{p_{0}^{3}}-\frac{2p_{\kappa}c}{p_{0}^{3}}\right]. (67) The bracket determines the normalization, while the explicit 1 / n 1/n factor gives σ ( C sample ) ∝ n − 1 / 2 \sigma(C_{\rm sample})\propto n^{-1/2} . If p κ ≃ p 0 = p p_{\kappa}\simeq p_{0}=p (as is typically the case, since | Δ ​ κ ​ C sample | = 𝒪 ⁡ ( 10 − 2 ) \lvert\Delta\kappa\,C_{\rm sample}\rvert=\mathcal{O}(10^{-2}) ) and the paired indicators have correlation coefficient ρ \rho , this reduces to σ ⁡ ( C sample ) ≃ 1 | Δ ​ κ | ​ 2 ​ ( 1 − ρ ) ​ ( 1 − p ) n ​ p . \sigma(C_{\rm sample})\simeq\frac{1}{|\Delta\kappa|}\sqrt{\frac{2(1-\rho)(1-p)}{np}}. (68) Thus rare selections have larger calibration noise, whereas positive covariance between paired fiducial and magnified outcomes reduces it. The actual Balrog estimator is weighted and combines galaxies with heterogeneous selection probabilities, so it is not exactly binomial. For a fixed heterogeneous population, its variance instead contains weighted sums of the individual p i ​ ( 1 − p i ) p_{i}(1-p_{i}) contributions. Provided the injected population and distribution of observing conditions remain fixed, these terms still decrease inversely with the effective number of independent attempts. The fitted amplitude A s A_{s} absorbs the selection efficiencies, weights, pairing covariance, and residual spatial correlations. A fixed-footprint jackknife may also contain an area-dependent component that does not continue to decrease as N inj − 1 / 2 N_{\rm inj}^{-1/2} , so the long-range extrapolations should not be interpreted as a complete error model. We leave these explorations to future work, but this back-of-the-envelope calculation already demonstrates that exquisite statistical precision in the calibration of the magnification response is achievable with a dedicated injection campaign.

sections.heading: Appendix B Robustness to redshift overlap
sections.text: The fiducial BigMag simulations have little overlap between the low-redshift foreground samples and the high-redshift magnification-selected samples. Their cross-correlations are therefore dominated by magnification. In real data, low-redshift tails in the background distributions also generate intrinsic galaxy clustering. Here we quantify how this contribution changes the signal and its positive/negative response pattern, and compare the controlled tests with the data-informed redshift distributions of Sec. 3 .

sections.heading: B.1 Controlled overlap tests
sections.text: We introduce a low-redshift component into each normalized background distribution according to n H j ϵ ′ ​ ( z ) = ( 1 − f overlap ) ​ n H j ϵ ​ ( z ) + f overlap ​ n L j ​ ( z ) , with ​ ϵ ∈ { + , − } , \begin{split}&n^{\prime}_{H_{j}^{\epsilon}}(z)=(1-f_{\rm overlap})n_{H_{j}^{\epsilon}}(z)+f_{\rm overlap}n_{L_{j}}(z),\\ &\text{with }\epsilon\in\{+,-\},\end{split} (69) with H 1 ± H_{1}^{\pm} matched to L 1 L_{1} , H 2 ± H_{2}^{\pm} to L 2 L_{2} , and H 3 ± H_{3}^{\pm} to L 3 L_{3} . The mapping defines a controlled tail shape; it does not imply that contaminants in the observed samples follow these particular foreground distributions. All foreground–background pairs are retained, including correlations with foreground bins other than the matched one. sections.heading: B.2 Comparison with the data-informed distributions
sections.text: We next examine the SOMPZ redshift distributions used to characterize the selections in Sec. 3 . The high-redshift population is first divided into three tomographic bins, and each bin is then split by magnification response. We evaluate the low-redshift tail separately for each parent bin and each response branch, using their respective redshift distributions. Specifically, F H j ϵ ​ ( z < 0.65 ) = ∫ 0 0.65 d ​ z ​ n ^ H j ϵ ​ ( z ) , F_{H_{j}^{\epsilon}}(z<0.65)=\int_{0}^{0.65}dz\,\hat{n}_{H_{j}^{\epsilon}}(z), (74) where n ^ \hat{n} has unit integral. For the tabulated SOMPZ distributions, this integral is evaluated by summing the normalized redshift-bin probabilities up to the bin edge at z = 0.65 z=0.65 . Table 5: Fractions below z = 0.65 z=0.65 in the data-informed SOMPZ redshift distributions. Parent denotes the unsplit population within each high-redshift tomographic bin; the other columns refer to its positive- and negative-response selections. These are total low-redshift tail fractions, not injected fractions or overlaps with an individual foreground bin. Bin Parent Positive response Negative response H 1 H_{1} 0.0123 0.0109 0.0128 H 2 H_{2} 0.0179 0.0129 0.0199 H 3 H_{3} 0.0232 0.0207 0.0253 The low-redshift fractions are therefore of order 1 1 – 3 % 3\% , with differences between the response branches that should be retained in a real-data model. However, these fractions cannot be identified directly with f overlap f_{\rm overlap} in the controlled scan. Equation ( 69 ) assigns the contaminating population a specific foreground-bin distribution, whereas the SOMPZ tails can be spread across the full low-redshift range. Two samples with the same F H ​ ( z < 0.65 ) F_{H}(z<0.65) can consequently have different overlaps with a given foreground bin and different intrinsic clustering signals. Predicting the intrinsic clustering contribution requires the full redshift distributions of both samples, together with their galaxy biases and the matter correlations. We therefore do not infer contamination signal-to-noise values for the data-informed samples by matching their total low-redshift tail fractions to the controlled scan. These tests show that percent-level overlap will not erase or wash out the magnification signal, but its impact must be assessed using the final low- and high-redshift data samples, including the separate positive- and negative-response selections. Minimizing their physical redshift overlap should be an explicit goal of sample optimization, alongside number density and magnification response. Any residual intrinsic clustering that cannot be shown to be negligible at the required precision should be included in the model, with uncertainties in the redshift tails and contaminant galaxy biases propagated into the cosmological constraints. For the tail shapes and biases considered here, f overlap ≤ 0.01 f_{\rm overlap}\leq 0.01 preserves all nine sign reversals, but this is not a universal tolerance: even at this overlap fraction, the density contribution has a signal-to-noise of approximately four. Also, preserving the sign reversal therefore does not by itself establish negligible cosmological bias. IGGL provides a complementary observable with a different sensitivity to these tails. Because it correlates the high-redshift galaxy positions with source shapes, it has no direct density–density contribution of the kind considered above. Its dominant magnification–shear signal also does not depend on the galaxy bias of the position sample. However, low-redshift contaminants in that sample can lie in front of the shape sources and generate a conventional galaxy–galaxy lensing contribution, while overlap with the shape-source distribution can introduce density–intrinsic-alignment correlations ( Cross and Sánchez, 2024 ) . The relevant redshift ordering must therefore be characterized using both the position and shape samples. Given the strong constraining power of IGGL in our forecasts, assessing these contributions for the final selections is particularly important: combining BigMag and IGGL offers complementary sensitivity to redshift-tail contamination, but does not remove the need to characterize and model it.

sections.heading: Appendix C Small-scale magnification ratios
sections.text: The fiducial BigMag analysis excludes projected separations below 4 ​ h − 1 ​ Mpc 4\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc} , where predicting the absolute clustering signal requires more detailed modeling of nonlinear galaxy bias and baryonic effects. Here we explore whether these measurements can instead constrain ratios of magnification responses or lensing efficiencies by cancelling the unknown small-scale galaxy–matter correlation. We write w i ​ j ϵ ​ ( θ ) ≡ w L i ​ H j ϵ ​ ( θ ) w_{ij}^{\epsilon}(\theta)\equiv w^{L_{i}H_{j}^{\epsilon}}(\theta) and C j ϵ ≡ C mag ​ ( H j ϵ ) C_{j}^{\epsilon}\equiv C^{\rm mag}(H_{j}^{\epsilon}) , with ϵ ∈ { + , − } \epsilon\in\{+,-\} . For negligible foreground–background redshift overlap, the leading magnification contribution is w i ​ j ϵ ​ ( θ ) ≃ C j ϵ ​ ⟨ δ g , i ​ κ j ⟩ ​ ( θ ) . w_{ij}^{\epsilon}(\theta)\simeq C_{j}^{\epsilon}\left\langle\delta_{g,i}\kappa_{j}\right\rangle(\theta). (75) Rather than dividing noisy measurements directly, we fit the original correlation functions with their joint covariance, profiling over nuisance amplitudes describing the unknown small-scale signal. These amplitudes are shared between the correlations whose common dependence is assumed to cancel. For positive- and negative-response samples with the same true redshift distribution, this construction measures R j − / + ≡ w i ​ j − ​ ( θ ) w i ​ j + ​ ( θ ) ≃ C j − C j + . R_{j}^{-/+}\equiv\frac{w_{ij}^{-}(\theta)}{w_{ij}^{+}(\theta)}\simeq\frac{C_{j}^{-}}{C_{j}^{+}}. (76) The common galaxy–matter correlation and lensing kernel cancel to leading order, so different foreground bins and angular scales provide repeated measurements of the same response ratio. However, multiplying both coefficients by a common factor leaves the ratio unchanged. These measurements therefore constrain the relative responses, but cannot determine their absolute normalization. Comparing samples of the same response sign at different source redshifts instead gives, in the narrow-foreground-bin limit, R i , j ​ k ϵ ≡ w i ​ j ϵ ​ ( θ ) w i ​ k ϵ ​ ( θ ) ≃ C j ϵ C k ϵ ​ β i ​ j β i ​ k , R_{i,jk}^{\epsilon}\equiv\frac{w_{ij}^{\epsilon}(\theta)}{w_{ik}^{\epsilon}(\theta)}\simeq\frac{C_{j}^{\epsilon}}{C_{k}^{\epsilon}}\frac{\beta_{ij}}{\beta_{ik}}, (77) where β i ​ j \beta_{ij} is the lensing efficiency averaged over the source redshift distribution. This ratio retains geometric information, analogously to conventional lensing ratios ( Prat et al., 2019 ) , but that information is degenerate with the relative responses and source redshift distributions. For our sample configuration, changing Ω m \Omega_{\rm m} from 0.3 0.3 to 0.2 0.2 or 0.4 0.4 changes the relevant distance ratios by only approximately 0.03 0.03 – 0.25 % 0.25\% , compared with statistical ratio uncertainties of approximately 3 3 – 8 % 8\% . The geometric sensitivity is therefore weak. We explored both constructions using the BigMag-only posterior with the fiducial response priors σ C = 0.2 \sigma_{C}=0.2 . A Gaussian covariance update predicts a reduction of less than 1 % 1\% in the marginalized fluctuation-amplitude uncertainty for either construction. Direct importance reweighting yields a low effective sample size because the ratio likelihoods select narrow directions in response space; apparent changes of several per cent in those reweighted constraints are consequently not robust. These exploratory results indicate no significant improvement in cosmological precision for the configuration considered here. The limited gain follows from the remaining absolute-response degeneracy. Even combining both constructions leaves all ratios unchanged under a global rescaling C j ϵ → λ ​ C j ϵ C_{j}^{\epsilon}\rightarrow\lambda C_{j}^{\epsilon} . This normalization remains degenerate with the cosmological lensing amplitude in the large-scale BigMag correlations. An absolute response calibration, for example from synthetic source injections, or complementary information from other observables is therefore still needed to constrain this mode. Small-scale ratios can thus complement absolute calibration by constraining relative responses and providing internal consistency tests. Their interpretation assumes sufficiently well-matched lensing kernels and control of residual redshift overlap and observational contamination. Because the two constructions use the same underlying correlations, a combined analysis must also retain their covariance, together with the covariance with the large-scale measurements.

text: Weak lensing, big magnification: Recovering hidden lensing information from galaxy positions Skip to main content Report GitHub Issue × Title: Content selection saved. Describe the issue below: Description: Why HTML? Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.03913v1 [astro-ph.CO] 02 Oct 2026 Weak lensing, big magnification: Recovering hidden lensing information from galaxy positions Alex Alarcon 1 Carles Sánchez 2,3 Affiliation: 1 Institute of Space Sciences (ICE, CSIC), Campus UAB, Carrer de Can Magrans, s/n, 08193 Barcelona, Spain Affiliation: 2 Departament de Física, Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona (UAB), 08193 Bellaterra (Barcelona), Spain Affiliation: 3 Institut de Física d’Altes Energies (IFAE), The Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology, Campus UAB, 08193 Bellaterra (Barcelona), Spain Abstract The combination of galaxy clustering and weak gravitational lensing is a powerful probe of cosmology, traditionally implemented through galaxy clustering and galaxy–galaxy lensing in a 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt analysis. An alternative lensing observable is the clustering cross-correlation of foreground and background galaxy samples induced by lensing magnification, but measurements of this signal have generally achieved lower signal-to-noise than shear-based lensing. We show that, for deep background samples selected from current photometric surveys, cancellation between galaxies with positive and negative magnification responses within the same sample can substantially reduce the achievable signal. Using DES Year 6 photometry and Balrog synthetic-source injections, we explore high-redshift ( z ≃ 0.7 z\simeq 0.7 – 2.5 2.5 ) galaxy samples split by the sign and amplitude of their magnification response. This separation reduces signal cancellation and can substantially increase both the magnification signal-to-noise and its cosmological constraining power. We refer to the resulting combination of foreground clustering and foreground–background cross-correlations with a response-selected background sample as BigMag. Forecasts based on DES-like simulated data vectors, adopting an optimistic sample configuration and sufficiently precise calibration of the magnification responses, show that BigMag can achieve constraining power comparable to traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt while relying only on galaxy positions. The same response-selected samples also enhance inverse galaxy–galaxy lensing (IGGL), a position–shear correlation dominated by magnification terms when the position sample lies behind the shape sample. Combining BigMag and IGGL self-calibrates the magnification responses further and yields marginalized S 8 S_{8} constraints comparable to traditional 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt analyses, and even tighter in the more precise magnification-calibration scenarios considered here. The framework also enables the construction of near-zero-magnification-response samples, with applications to traditional 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt and geometric lensing-ratio analyses. These results motivate further optimization and validation of galaxy selections to realize the potential of magnification as a complementary probe of cosmology. keywords methods: data analysis - gravitational lensing: weak - catalogs - surveys 1 Introduction Modern imaging surveys contain hundreds of millions of detected galaxies ( Bechtol et al., 2026 ) , and forthcoming experiments will increase this number to several billion ( Ivezić et al., 2019 ; Akeson et al., 2019 ; Euclid Collaboration et al., 2025c ; CSST Collaboration et al., 2026 ) . Yet only a fraction of these objects typically enter cosmological analyses ( DES Collaboration et al., 2026 , e.g.,) . The requirements imposed on a galaxy sample depend strongly on the observable for which it is used. Galaxy samples used for clustering (often referred to as lens or position samples) are generally restricted to relatively bright galaxies at low or intermediate redshift ( Weaverdyck et al., 2026 ) . Their observed number density can correlate with survey depth, seeing, sky brightness, stellar density, and other observing conditions. Because their autocorrelations are used to constrain galaxy bias and cosmology, these spatial variations must be accurately characterized and mitigated ( Rodríguez-Monroy et al., 2025 ) . Galaxy samples used for weak lensing shear (usually called source or shape samples) can extend to substantially fainter objects and higher redshifts, but require reliable galaxy shape measurements, shear calibration, and redshift characterization ( Yamamoto et al., 2025 ) . These requirements exclude many detected galaxies from either role. Weak lensing magnification offers a complementary way to exploit this broader galaxy population. By changing the observed solid angle and altering the apparent fluxes and sizes of background galaxies ( Bartelmann, 2010 ; Prat and Bacon, 2026 ) , magnification modulates their observed number density and the probability that they enter a selected sample. This signal can be isolated by cross-correlating foreground and background populations with minimal redshift overlap: physical clustering is then strongly suppressed, leaving a correlation dominated by the magnification of background galaxies by matter traced by the foreground sample. Like galaxy-galaxy lensing, this observable probes the foreground galaxy-matter connection, but uses background galaxy positions rather than shapes. Because the background population enters only through cross-correlations, its autocorrelation need not be modeled; provided the foreground density field is adequately corrected and residual imaging fluctuations are not correlated between the samples, background systematics increase the variance without biasing the mean signal. The background selection can therefore extend to deeper, denser samples, including galaxies without usable shapes, while the foreground sample remains subject to the usual clustering-systematics requirements. This work focuses on magnification-induced position–position correlations, which have been measured using a range of background populations ( Scranton et al., 2005 ; Hildebrandt et al., 2009 ; Morrison et al., 2012 ; Garcia-Fernandez et al., 2018 ; González-Nuevo et al., 2014 ) . Although well established, such measurements have generally achieved lower signal-to-noise than shape-based weak-lensing measurements ( Bernstein, 2009 ; Bartelmann, 2010 ; van Waerbeke, 2010 ; Joachimi and Bridle, 2010 ; Duncan et al., 2014 ; Mahony et al., 2022 ; Cueli et al., 2025 ) . One important and avoidable source of this reduced statistical power, recognised since the earliest quasar–galaxy analyses ( Ménard and Bartelmann, 2002 ) , is cancellation within conventionally selected background samples. A selected population responds through two competing effects: expansion of the observed area dilutes its surface density, while magnification of galaxy fluxes and sizes changes the number of objects satisfying the selection ( von Wietersheim-Kramsta et al., 2021 ; Elvin-Poole et al., 2023 ; Legnani et al., 2026 ) . The net response can therefore be positive, negative, or close to zero, and a conventional sample may combine populations with opposite responses whose lensing signals partially cancel. Separating these populations preserves the oppositely signed contributions and also helps distinguish magnification from residual intrinsic clustering: the magnification signal reverses sign between the samples, whereas clustering caused by redshift overlap does not ( Hildebrandt et al., 2009 , e.g.) . Crucially, the magnification response is a property that can be estimated before measuring the cosmological cross-correlation. Catalogue-level perturbations have been used to propagate artificial magnification through the complex selection of spectroscopic samples and through flux-dependent photometric-redshift assignment ( Wenzl et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2025a ) . Image-level synthetic-source injection methods, such as Balrog , extend this logic through detection and measurement: simulated galaxies are magnified by a known amount, injected into real survey images, and processed through the same detection, measurement, and selection pipeline as the data ( Suchyta et al., 2016 ; Everett et al., 2022 ; Anbajagane et al., 2025 ) . The change in the number of selected objects then provides a direct calibration of the sample-selection response ( Elvin-Poole et al., 2023 ; Legnani et al., 2026 ) . A self-organizing map (SOM) ( Myles et al., 2021 ; Giannini et al., 2025 ; Yin et al., 2025 ) offers a natural representation of this information: cells containing galaxies with similar observed colors and magnitudes can be assigned both a redshift distribution and a magnification response. The SOM can then be used to construct high-redshift samples whose responses have a controlled sign and amplitude while maintaining the required redshift separation from the foreground sample. In this work, we use injection-calibrated responses not only to calibrate a given selection but to define it. We split high-redshift galaxy samples into populations with positive and negative net magnification responses in the multi-dimensional colour–magnitude space of the SOM. Treating these populations as separate density fields prevents their signals from cancelling and provides cross-correlations with opposite signs around the same foreground structures. We call the combination of foreground clustering and its cross-correlation with these dense, response-optimized background samples BigMag. Its structure closely parallels that of a traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt analysis ( Porredon et al., 2022 ; Pandey et al., 2022 ) . In both cases, the foreground autocorrelation constrains the combination of galaxy bias and matter clustering, while a lensing cross-correlation breaks the degeneracy between galaxy bias and the cosmological fluctuation amplitude. Traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt uses galaxy–galaxy lensing for this purpose; BigMag instead uses magnification-induced correlations between galaxy positions. The amplitude calibration provided by the magnification coefficient consequently plays a role analogous (although not identical) to the multiplicative shear calibration in galaxy–galaxy lensing. The same response-selected high-redshift samples also enhance inverse galaxy–galaxy lensing (IGGL) ( Cross and Sánchez, 2024 ) . In the IGGL configuration, the galaxy-position sample lies behind the source-shape sample. The conventional density–shear contribution is then strongly suppressed, and the position–shear correlation is dominated by the correlation between the magnification of the high-redshift position sample and the shear of the foreground source sample, together with the corresponding intrinsic-alignment contribution. BigMag and IGGL depend on the same magnification coefficients but probe them through different correlations and redshift kernels. Their combination can therefore partially self-calibrate the magnification responses while simultaneously constraining cosmology. It also provides a valuable consistency test because the two observables have different dependencies on galaxy bias, shear calibration, intrinsic alignments, and observational systematics. We demonstrate this approach using DES Year 6 photometry, Balrog synthetic-source injections, and SOM-based redshift calibration to construct galaxy selections with controlled redshift distributions and magnification responses. We then use DES-informed number densities, redshift distributions, and response coefficients to generate simulated clustering and weak-lensing data vectors. These forecasts quantify the gain from separating positive- and negative-response populations, compare BigMag with traditional 2 × 2 2\times 2 pt, and study the additional information supplied by IGGL. We also compare the combined magnification observables with cosmic shear and standard 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt analyses. Finally, we investigate the calibration precision required for the magnification coefficients, the sensitivity of the measurement to residual redshift overlap, and the information available from magnification ratios on scales excluded from the fiducial cosmological analysis. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the magnification contribution to galaxy-density correlations, motivates response-based sample selection, and discusses IGGL and sensitivity to observational systematics. Section 3 presents the DES Year 6 and Balrog data products, explores magnitude- and SOM-based selections, and describes the simulated data vectors. Section 4 presents the cosmological forecasts for BigMag and IGGL and their comparison and combination with traditional weak-lensing probes. We then discuss the implications and requirements for applying the method to data and summarize our conclusions. The appendices provide further tests of magnification-response selection and calibration, assess the impact of redshift overlap, explore small-scale magnification ratios, and derive the treatment of a redshift-dependent magnification response. 2 Theory and motivation This section develops the theoretical framework for the magnification observables used in this work. We describe how intrinsic clustering and weak-lensing magnification contribute to galaxy density correlations, motivating background-galaxy selections based on their magnification response. We then discuss magnification in galaxy–galaxy lensing, focusing on the inverse configuration, and assess the impact of observational systematics. 2.1 Galaxy density and magnification bias In large-scale structure surveys, the observed angular distribution of galaxies is used to trace the underlying matter density field through galaxy clustering measurements. In the absence of lensing effects, the intrinsic galaxy density contrast in tomographic bin i i can be written as the line-of-sight projection of the three-dimensional galaxy density field, δ g , i int ​ ( 𝐧 ^ ) = ∫ d ​ χ ​ W g i ​ ( χ ) ​ δ g 3 ​ D ​ ( 𝐧 ^ ​ χ , χ ) , \delta_{g,i}^{\mathrm{int}}(\hat{\mathbf{n}})=\int d\chi\,W_{g}^{i}(\chi)\,\delta_{g}^{3\mathrm{D}}(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\chi,\chi), (1) where χ \chi is the comoving distance and W g i ​ ( χ ) W_{g}^{i}(\chi) denotes the normalized redshift selection function of the galaxy sample. Equation ( 10 ) shows explicitly that magnification affects the observed galaxy density through two competing contributions. The first term, C area = − 2 C_{\mathrm{area}}=-2 , arises from the stretching of the sky area and always acts to dilute the observed number density. The second term, C sample C_{\mathrm{sample}} , reflects the response of the galaxy selection to lensing-induced changes in observed fluxes and sizes. Because magnification increases the apparent flux and size of background galaxies while simultaneously diluting their surface density, the net sign and amplitude of the magnification-induced overdensity depend on the balance between these effects. For flux-limited samples, this balance is governed by the slope of the cumulative luminosity function ( Joachimi and Bridle, 2010 ; Garcia-Fernandez et al., 2018 , e.g.) : steep slopes enhance the flux-boosting term and can lead to a positive magnification response, whereas shallow slopes result in a net suppression of the observed density.
