In this configuration, the auto-correlation primarily constrains the galaxy bias of the foreground sample, while the cross-correlation isolates the magnification-induced signal that probes the matter distribution along the line of sight and depends linearly on the magnification coefficient of the background galaxies. Two key implications follow from this framework, which form the main motivation for the analysis presented in this paper: • The magnification coefficient of background galaxies, which sets the amplitude (and sign) of the cross-correlation signal, can be estimated a priori for galaxy samples using synthetic source injection (SSI) techniques, such as Balrog . This enables the design and optimisation of sample selections that maximise the magnification signal, an aspect that is particularly important in the presence of mixed populations that would otherwise lead to partial cancellation between negative and positive magnification contributions. We explore this strategy in detail in § 2.3 . • Because the analysis does not require the auto-correlation of the background sample, the cosmological inference is significantly less sensitive to observational systematics affecting that sample. This relaxes the requirements on systematics mitigation for the background galaxies, allowing for more aggressive selections and the inclusion of a larger number of objects. The impact of observational systematics in this context is discussed in § 2.5 . 2.3 Optimizing galaxy selections for magnification C sample = 2 C_{\mathrm{sample}}=2 null × \times -corr. negative × \times -corr. positive × \times -corr. Building on the framework above, we now consider how background-galaxy selections can be designed to enhance sensitivity to magnification. Because the magnification-induced cross-correlation scales linearly with C mag C_{\mathrm{mag}} , Eq. ( 13 ), broad selections can combine galaxies with positive, negative, and near-zero responses whose contributions partially cancel, reducing the signal-to-noise ratio (Figure 2 ). This motivates grouping background galaxies according to the sign and magnitude of C mag C_{\mathrm{mag}} , so that their contributions add coherently. Since C mag C_{\mathrm{mag}} can be characterized using sample-selection response techniques such as synthetic source injections, these response-based selections can be constructed and optimized in practice. The principle is the same as in ( α − 1 ) (\alpha-1) -weighted estimators ( Ménard and Bartelmann, 2002 ; Scranton et al., 2005 ) , here applied to responses calibrated for arbitrary selections rather than inferred from the number-count slope, and with the resulting groups kept as separate fields rather than combined into a single weighted sample. Figure 3 illustrates this gain using a simulated clustering cross-correlation between foreground and background samples at z = 0.34 z=0.34 and z = 1.7 z=1.7 , like those from Fig. 1 , with number densities informed by DES Y6 (more details about this in § 3 ). In the absence of magnification, the cross-correlation of the foreground and background samples is null, as expected, since they do not overlap in redshift. When considering magnification, an unsplit background sample, like the one depicted in Fig. 2 , produces a magnification signal with modest signal-to-noise because of partial cancellation (left panel). Splitting the same background parent population into subsamples with positive and negative magnification responses substantially increases the signal-to-noise of the measurement (right panel). The construction of these samples from real data is described in § 3 . Opposite-response subsamples also provide an internal consistency test of the origin of the signal. The leading magnification-induced correlation changes sign with C mag C_{\rm mag} , whereas obscuration and dust extinction dim background galaxies ( Ménard et al., 2010 ) and can reduce the observed background counts without following this sign reversal ( Hildebrandt et al., 2013 ; Gaztanaga et al., 2021 ) . Comparing subsamples around the same foreground galaxies, while accounting for differences in their redshift distributions and selection, can therefore help distinguish magnification from observational contamination. On the other hand, samples with C mag ≃ 0 C_{\rm mag}\simeq 0 provide a complementary null test of the leading magnification contribution, and they would also have applications beyond these consistency tests. The same response-calibration and selection machinery used here to enhance magnification can instead be used to construct samples with a total magnification response close to zero in each tomographic bin. Applied to the galaxy-position samples in 3 × 2 3\times 2 pt analyses, this would suppress lens-magnification contributions to galaxy clustering and galaxy–galaxy lensing, reducing their sensitivity to magnification modelling and response-calibration uncertainties ( Euclid Collaboration et al., 2022 ; Elvin-Poole et al., 2023 ; Legnani et al., 2026 ) . Furthermore, null-response lens samples would be particularly valuable for lensing ratio measurements ( Jain and Taylor, 2003 ; Prat et al., 2019 ; Unruh et al., 2019 ) , where the contributions from magnification can reduce the geometrical nature that makes these measurements so interesting. Having established the motivation for response-based selections, we next discuss their relevance to inverse galaxy–galaxy lensing and the impact of observational systematics on these observables. 2.4 (Inverse) Galaxy-galaxy lensing Another measurement that can be dominated by weak lensing magnification in particular redshift configurations is galaxy-galaxy lensing (GGL, Kaiser 1992 ). In practice, the observed galaxy density field is affected by observational systematics arising from spatial variations of survey depth, seeing, sky brightness, stellar contamination, and other imaging-related effects.
